projectTitle: Brennan Manufacturing: High Availability That's Actually Tested, Start to Finish
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of real on-prem SQL Server high availability — Windows clustering, AlwaysOn Availability Groups, performance tuning, and automation — for one fictional manufacturer, closing with multi-platform discipline extended to an ungoverned MongoDB database.
businessContext:
**Brennan Manufacturing** is a fictional mid-size industrial manufacturer whose core ERP/production-scheduling database ran for 9 years on a single on-premises SQL Server (`SQLPROD01`) with nightly backups and no real high availability. A recent hardware failure took that server down for 48 hours, costing a dozen missed ship dates and hours of production changeover — and finally got leadership to fund real resilience. You've been brought in as a SQL Server DBA to build it right: a genuine two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster with a synchronous-commit AlwaysOn Availability Group, real performance tuning, real automation via the open-source `dbatools` toolkit, an off-site backup copy in Azure, and — as your responsibility over the company's database estate grows — bringing an ungoverned MongoDB database a product team spun up under the same real DBA discipline.

This series follows that build end to end — including a real incident where a routine, reasonable DBA task (creating a new database for a new module) quietly left that database outside the Availability Group, undiscovered until the first real failover test finally ran.
architectureSummary: By the end of this series, Brennan Manufacturing has: a two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster (`SQLDBA01`/`SQLDBA02`) with a cloud witness for quorum; a synchronous-commit, automatic-failover AlwaysOn Availability Group (`BrennanAG`) behind a single listener (`BrennanAGListener`) that the ERP application connects through; `dbatools`-based PowerShell automation for backups, restore verification, and maintenance; a tuned production-scheduling query with a real missing-index fix; off-site backups to Azure Blob Storage via native backup-to-URL; AG and job-failure monitoring; a MongoDB instance brought under real backup/access/monitoring discipline; and a real incident — a new database that was never added to the Availability Group, found during a failover test, fixed, and now caught automatically by a recurring AG-membership check. Nothing here is more advanced than the tools taught earlier in this path — the point of this series is showing how Windows clustering, AlwaysOn, dbatools, Azure backup, and cross-platform discipline fit together on one real job, not introducing new tools.

lessons.title: Meeting Brennan Manufacturing: Why Nobody Trusts the Backup Plan
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: a 48-hour outage on a single aging SQL Server froze production scheduling for two days, and what you have to learn before you design anything to replace it.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll walk through one complete, start-to-finish SQL Server DBA engagement for a fictional mid-size industrial manufacturer, **Brennan Manufacturing** -- a single plant running three production lines, roughly 450 customer orders moving through the shop floor every month, and one core database, `BrennanERP`, that holds production scheduling, work orders, and order fulfillment for the whole plant. That database has run on a single on-premises SQL Server, `SQLPROD01`, for nine years, backed up nightly and nothing else. You've been brought in to build real resilience around it: a genuine two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster, a SQL Server AlwaysOn Availability Group with automatic failover, real performance tuning, PowerShell automation with the dbatools toolkit, an off-site backup copy in Azure Storage, and -- later in this same engagement, once that foundation is solid -- bringing a MongoDB database the product team stood up on its own under the same real DBA discipline.

By the end of this series, Brennan Manufacturing has a cluster that's been proven with a real failover, not just configured and assumed to work, backups that are verified rather than hoped-for, and a DBA practice that covers more than one relational engine. This video starts exactly where that work has to start: not with a cluster, not with a single line of T-SQL, but with the meeting where you find out precisely what happened during the outage that got this project funded in the first place.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine two kids share one bicycle to deliver the neighborhood newspaper every morning. One bike, one route, and it's worked fine for years. Then one morning the bike's chain snaps in a spot nobody can fix at home, and the replacement part has to be ordered and shipped. For two whole days, no papers get delivered at all -- not because anyone forgot to do their job, but because there was only ever one bike and no plan for what happens when it breaks.

That's exactly what happened at Brennan Manufacturing, except instead of a bicycle, it's the one computer that tells the factory floor what to build next and in what order. When that computer's hard-drive controller failed, nobody could even look up what orders were due, let alone finish them, until a replacement part arrived two days later. Before you build anything new, your very first job is to sit down with the people who lived through those two days and find out exactly what went wrong -- because you can't design a cure for a problem you haven't actually diagnosed.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery meeting, and the detail that matters most isn't the headline -- "the server went down for two days" -- it's the specific chain of single points of failure underneath that headline, because that chain tells you exactly what the new design has to eliminate. A failed RAID controller on a nine-year-old server is not a freak event; it's the predictable outcome of running one box, with no secondary copy of the database anywhere that could take over, for nearly a decade. What makes this worth a full discovery meeting rather than a one-line ticket is how badly a single piece of hardware was allowed to become the one thing standing between the shop floor and total scheduling blindness.

You'll hear this story from three different vantage points, and each one surfaces a different real requirement. Dana Kowalski, Brennan's VP of Operations, cares about this never happening again and about having a real, tested answer the next time leadership asks "what's our plan if this breaks." Marcus Webb, the Production Manager, cares about something narrower and just as real: his line supervisors run the floor off whatever `BrennanERP` tells them is due next, and without it they're sequencing work from memory and a whiteboard. And Greg Hollis, the IT generalist who has personally kept `SQLPROD01` alive for most of its nine years without ever being a dedicated DBA, knows the detail nobody wants to say in the first five minutes of the meeting: the nightly backups were current, but a real restore to new hardware had never actually been rehearsed, and that's most of why the outage lasted two days instead of two hours.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Know the failure chain before you walk into the room

Don't open a discovery meeting with "what happened?" and stop there. Come in already prepared to ask the follow-up questions, because the first answer is never the whole story:

- What component actually failed, and was it the only warning sign, or had something else already been flagged and ignored?
- How old is the server, and when was the hardware itself last refreshed or inspected?
- How current was the last good backup when the failure happened, and how was that backup actually verified?
- Had a full restore to different hardware ever been tested end to end before this incident forced one?
- Is there any secondary copy of this database anywhere, on any server, that could have taken over?

## Step 2 -- Run the meeting and let the real numbers surface

Dana Kowalski, VP of Operations, opens with the headline:

```
DANA:   Nine-year-old server, one failed RAID controller, and we were
        completely blind on production scheduling for two full days
        while we waited on a replacement part. That's the two days
        that finally got this project a real budget, and I want you
        to hear exactly what happened from Greg before we talk about
        fixing anything.
```

Greg Hollis, who has been the de facto administrator of `SQLPROD01` for most of its life without ever having dedicated DBA tooling or a second server to fail over to, fills in the chain:

```
GREG:   The RAID controller card failed outright on a Thursday
        afternoon. It's a single server, direct-attached storage, no
        second node anywhere -- so when that card died, the whole box
        was unreachable. The replacement card had to be special-ordered
        from the manufacturer; it didn't land until Saturday morning.

YOU:    Walk me through the backups. What were you actually restoring
        from, and how old was it?

GREG:   Full backup every night at 11pm, nothing in between -- no log
        shipping, no second copy anywhere else. So worst case we lost
        whatever changed between 11pm Thursday and whenever the card
        actually failed Thursday afternoon -- turned out to be about
        four hours of order updates. The part that actually cost us
        the second day wasn't the backup, it was the restore. I'd
        never done a full bare-metal restore of this database before.
        Once the loaner server arrived, it took most of a day just to
        get SQL Server installed, patched, and the database restored
        and verified -- because I was working it out as I went.

MARCUS: And that's the part that hit the floor. My three lines run off
        whatever BrennanERP says is due next. For two days we were
        sequencing jobs off a whiteboard and whoever remembered what
        was promised to who. We missed ship dates on twelve orders,
        and one line lost about six hours to changeovers we'd have
        skipped if we'd had the real schedule in front of us.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the incident summary while it's still fresh

```
BRENNAN MANUFACTURING -- INCIDENT SUMMARY (DISCOVERY INPUT)

What happened:      RAID controller failure on SQLPROD01, the sole
                     server hosting BrennanERP. No secondary server,
                     no failover path of any kind.
Outage duration:     ~48 hours (failure Thursday afternoon; replacement
                     part and restore not complete until Saturday).
Data loss exposure:  ~4 hours of order/schedule updates, based on an
                     11pm nightly full-backup schedule with no log
                     backups in between.
Untested assumption: A full bare-metal restore to new hardware had
                     never been rehearsed before this incident forced one.
Business impact:     12 orders missed their ship date; one production
                     line lost ~6 hours to avoidable changeovers while
                     running off a whiteboard schedule.
Server age:          9 years old, single server, direct-attached
                     storage, no secondary site or node.
```

## Step 4 -- Get the story confirmed in writing

Send this summary to Dana, Marcus, and Greg and ask each one directly: "Is this an accurate account of what happened and what was at risk?" That confirmation matters later -- every testable requirement you write in the next lesson traces back to a specific line in this document, and it's what you'll point back to the day a real failover test proves (or doesn't yet prove) that this can't happen again.

The restore itself -- not the backup -- is what turned a hardware failure into a 48-hour outage. That's exactly the gap a real two-node cluster with automatic failover closes.

This project exists to make sure that specific failure -- one server, no backup path to keep running -- can never cause that again.

lessons.title: Turning 'Make It Resilient' Into a Testable Availability Requirement
lessons.summary: Converting Dana's 'make it resilient' and the incident numbers into specific RPO/RTO targets, a verified-backup requirement, and a performance baseline the project can actually be judged against.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The discovery meeting gave you a real incident and three honest accounts of what went wrong -- but "make it resilient" and "we can't have this happen again" aren't requirements yet, they're intentions. This lesson turns them into numbers you can actually design against: a Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective pulled directly out of the Lesson 1 incident summary, a concrete definition of what "the backup is good" actually means going forward, and a performance baseline so that once the new cluster exists, you can prove -- not just assume -- that it's at least as fast as `SQLPROD01` ever was.

This is the document every later decision in this series answers to. When the Windows Server Failover Cluster gets built, when `BrennanAG` and `BrennanAGListener` get configured, when dbatools automation gets scripted, and when all of it eventually gets tested with a real failover drill, each piece traces back to a specific, numbered line in the document you write in this lesson -- not to a vague memory of Dana saying she wanted things "more reliable."
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the two kids sharing one bicycle? After the two-day newspaper disaster, everyone agrees they want things to be "more reliable." But "more reliable" doesn't tell anyone what to actually build. Does it mean a second bike sitting ready in the garage? Does it mean someone can take over mid-route in under a minute, or is five minutes okay? Until somebody writes the actual numbers down, two people can both say "yes, that's reliable now" about two completely different setups.

That's what this lesson does for Brennan Manufacturing. "Make it resilient" turns into real numbers: if something breaks, how many minutes of data can we afford to lose, and how fast do we have to be back up and running on the floor? Once those numbers exist, you, Dana, Marcus, and Greg are all building toward the exact same target instead of three different guesses at what "resilient" means.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A requirement that can't be falsified isn't a requirement, it's a hope -- and hope is precisely what Brennan Manufacturing was running on when `SQLPROD01`'s controller card died. The two numbers that matter most for any high-availability design are Recovery Point Objective, how much committed data can we afford to lose, and Recovery Time Objective, how long can the floor tolerate being without a live schedule. Both should come straight out of what discovery already told you: the incident summary's roughly four-hour exposure window under the old nightly-only backup regime is your honest baseline for how bad "no real plan" actually was, and Marcus's numbers give you a concrete way to express what a missed ship date actually costs on the floor.

Those old numbers also tell you exactly what a synchronous AlwaysOn Availability Group buys over the status quo: inside `BrennanWSFC`, a synchronous-commit secondary on `SQLDBA02` means a committed transaction on `SQLDBA01` is already written to the secondary before the application gets its acknowledgment, which drives the in-cluster RPO down near zero rather than down to "however many hours since the last backup." RTO for an in-cluster failover through `BrennanAGListener` is a matter of seconds to low minutes, not days -- but that number is only real once a failover has actually been executed and timed, not just configured and trusted. A separate, more conservative RTO still has to be written down for a true disaster-recovery scenario -- the whole site, cluster included, being unavailable and a restore from the off-site Azure backup copy being the only path back -- because that scenario is real and slower by design, and pretending the fast in-cluster number covers it would be dishonest. Performance needs the same discipline: you cannot credibly claim the new cluster performs as well as or better than `SQLPROD01` without first capturing what `SQLPROD01` actually does today, on real production-scheduling queries, under a real daily load.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull every testable number out of what you already know

```
FROM DISCOVERY (Lesson 1):
  - Nightly full backup only, ~4 hours of exposure in the actual incident
  - A bare-metal restore had never been rehearsed before being forced
  - Outage lasted ~48 hours; 12 orders missed ship date; one line lost
    ~6 hours to avoidable changeovers
  - Server (SQLPROD01) is 9 years old with no secondary node at all
```

## Step 2 -- Draft two separate RPO/RTO pairs, and defend each one

```
IN-CLUSTER FAILOVER (BrennanWSFC / BrennanAG / BrennanAGListener):
  RPO: near-zero (seconds) for committed transactions, achieved via
       synchronous-commit availability mode between SQLDBA01 and
       SQLDBA02.
  RTO: under 60 seconds for an automatic failover through
       BrennanAGListener, measured by an actual timed drill, not
       assumed from the configuration alone.
  Why: the old environment lost ~4 hours of data because there was no
       second copy anywhere; a synchronous secondary in the same
       cluster removes that exposure almost entirely.

SITE-LEVEL DISASTER RECOVERY (restore from brennansqlbackups):
  RPO: up to 15 minutes, based on the off-site backup-to-URL cadence
       planned for Azure Storage.
  RTO: a documented, rehearsed restore window measured in hours, not
       days -- explicitly slower than the in-cluster number, and
       explicitly not confused with it.
  Why: BrennanWSFC itself, or the whole building, failing is a real
       scenario the cluster alone does not protect against.
```

## Step 3 -- Turn "the backup is good" into a checkable requirement

```
BACKUP-1: Every production backup is verified, not just completed.
          Verification method: Test-DbaLastBackup (dbatools) run on a
          schedule, restoring each backup to a scratch instance and
          confirming it's actually usable -- the exact step that was
          missing before this incident.
BACKUP-2: An off-site copy of every full and log backup lands in the
          brennansqlbackups Azure Storage account automatically, so a
          single-site disaster doesn't also destroy the backups.
```

## Step 4 -- Turn "is it fast enough" into a baseline-first requirement

```
PERF-1: Before the new cluster goes live, capture real baseline
        numbers from SQLPROD01 today -- the specific scheduling and
        order-lookup queries Marcus's team actually runs, and how long
        they currently take.
        Why first: without this number, nobody can later prove the new
        AG-backed environment performs as well as or better than what
        it replaced -- "it feels fine" isn't a verification method.
```

## Step 5 -- Review it line by line with Dana, Marcus, and Greg

Read each requirement aloud and ask for a direct yes or no. Greg in particular needs to hear the in-cluster vs. disaster-recovery distinction clearly -- it's easy to assume the fast AG failover number covers every bad scenario, and it doesn't.

## Step 6 -- Decide who owns verifying each number, on an actual cadence

A requirement with no owner and no schedule quietly turns back into a hope within a few months. Write the ownership down alongside the number:

```
REQUIREMENT                 VERIFIED BY           CADENCE
In-cluster RPO/RTO           You (DBA), via a      Timed failover drill,
                             logged failover test   at least quarterly
BACKUP-1 (restorable)        Test-DbaLastBackup     Nightly, automated,
                             (dbatools), scheduled   with alerting on
                             via SQL Agent or        failure
                             a PowerShell job
BACKUP-2 (off-site copy)     Storage account         Weekly spot-check,
                             activity log review      automated where possible
PERF-1 baseline              You, compared against   Re-run after any major
                             the original capture     cluster or schema change
```

Greg takes first pass at day-to-day monitoring once automation is in place; you retain ownership of the quarterly drill itself, since that's the one check nobody should be able to quietly skip when things feel calm.

## Step 7 -- Version and date the requirements document

Save it as `Brennan_V1_Availability_Requirements_v1.md`. This is the document Lesson 3 uses to draw the scope line, and the document the eventual failover drill gets measured against.

Added Test-DbaLastBackup as the actual verification method for 'the backup is good,' and a baseline-first performance requirement against SQLPROD01's current queries.

This is what the cluster build and the eventual go-live testing both get measured against.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'make this resilient' into specific commitments: a hardware failure inside the cluster now costs seconds, not two days, and even a worst-case scenario where the whole building is affected has a rehearsed, bounded recovery plan instead of an improvised one. Backups are being verified as restorable, not just assumed to be good because they completed.

lessons.title: Scoping V1: High Availability and Performance Now, Multi-Platform Next
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard line around what phase one delivers -- the cluster, the Availability Group, performance tuning, and automation -- and scoping the MongoDB oversight work as this same engagement's next phase, not a separate promise.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
You now have real, numbered availability and performance requirements. Before a single server gets racked or a cluster feature gets enabled, this lesson draws a hard written line around what V1 of this engagement actually covers. For Brennan Manufacturing, that line is specific: V1 delivers a genuine two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster, `BrennanWSFC`, carrying a SQL Server AlwaysOn Availability Group, `BrennanAG`, with `BrennanERP` protected from day one and reachable through `BrennanAGListener`; a captured performance baseline and the tuning work that follows it; and real PowerShell automation built on dbatools for backups, verification, and routine maintenance, so none of this depends on Greg remembering to run a script by hand. V1 also includes the off-site backup copy to the `brennansqlbackups` Azure Storage account, because a cluster that protects against hardware failure but still has only one copy of its backups sitting in the same building isn't actually finished.

What's explicitly scoped as the next phase of this same engagement -- not a separate future project, not dropped -- is bringing a MongoDB database, `brennan-mongo-01` running `iot_sensor_logs`, under the same real DBA discipline. A product team stood that database up on its own for a new IoT sensor-logging feature with no DBA involvement at all, and it genuinely needs backups, monitoring, and an access review. That work is coming later in this same engagement, once the relational foundation -- HA, performance, and automation -- is solid enough that attention can safely move to a second platform.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you just finished building a much sturdier treehouse after the old one lost a board in a storm. While you're up there with your tools, your cousin mentions there's also an old shed out back that nobody's checked on in months -- it might have a leaky roof too. You don't stop building the treehouse to go fix the shed right this second. You finish the treehouse properly first, because that's the thing that actually broke, and then you go check on the shed next, as part of the very same weekend of work -- not some separate trip you might get to someday.

That's exactly the plan for Brennan Manufacturing. The treehouse is the SQL Server cluster -- that's what actually broke and that's what gets built first. The shed is a MongoDB database a different team set up on their own, with nobody checking on it. It's real, it matters, and it's part of this same project -- it's just next, not first.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline matters here because the two platforms genuinely compete for the same attention, and bundling them together on day one would slow down the thing that actually caused a 48-hour outage: a single SQL Server with no failover path. The discipline is the same one from the requirements lesson -- every idea on the table gets an explicit, written disposition, not a shrug -- but the stakes are different, because `brennan-mongo-01` isn't a hypothetical nice-to-have. It's a real, already-running database that a product team provisioned for an IoT sensor-logging feature without any DBA oversight, which means right now it likely has no tested backup, no monitoring, and an access list nobody has reviewed. Deferring it to V2 has to come with an honest acknowledgment of that exposure, not a pretense that it's low-risk because it's not SQL Server.

The sequencing logic is what makes the deferral defensible rather than just convenient: `BrennanERP` is the system that stops the shop floor cold when it's unavailable, so proving HA, capturing a performance baseline, and automating backup verification for it is the higher-priority fire. Once `BrennanWSFC` and `BrennanAG` are built, tested with a real failover, and running on dbatools-driven automation instead of manual effort, the same DBA attention and the same automation-first mindset extend naturally to `brennan-mongo-01` -- confirming real backups exist, setting up monitoring, and reviewing who actually has access to `iot_sensor_logs`. Writing that sequence down now, as a committed phase of this one engagement rather than a someday-maybe, is what keeps it from quietly becoming the next unmonitored system that fails without warning.

lessons.title: Choosing the Stack: AlwaysOn Availability Groups, Not Just Nightly Backups
lessons.summary: The first real architecture decision: why a synchronous AlwaysOn Availability Group across a two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster beats log shipping, mirroring, and a shared-storage cluster alone -- and the exact resource names this series uses from here forward.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked, this is the first real architecture decision: exactly how `BrennanERP` gets protected against the kind of single-server failure that cost Brennan Manufacturing two days of production visibility. SQL Server offers several real high-availability mechanisms here -- log shipping, database mirroring (deprecated, and worth naming as a reason on its own), a Failover Cluster Instance relying on one shared storage array, and an AlwaysOn Availability Group spanning independently-owned storage on each node. This lesson walks through why an Availability Group, built on top of a genuine two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster, is the right fit for this specific failure history and this requirement set -- not because it's the newest option, but because it's the one that actually closes the exact gap the Lesson 1 incident exposed: one server, one storage array, nothing to take over when either one fails.

This lesson also fixes the exact naming this whole engagement uses from here forward: the two nodes `SQLDBA01` (primary replica) and `SQLDBA02` (secondary replica), joined into the Windows Server Failover Cluster `BrennanWSFC`, carrying the Availability Group `BrennanAG` and its listener `BrennanAGListener`, with `BrennanERP` added to `BrennanAG` from day one. Every later lesson in this series refers back to these exact names.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about the two kids and their one bicycle again. After the big two-day delivery disaster, a few different fixes get suggested. One idea: keep one bike, but write the route down really carefully so a backup rider could follow it later if needed -- that's like log shipping, a copy that's always a little behind. Another idea: have two kids share one bike seat bolted to two sets of pedals, but it's still fundamentally one bike frame -- if that frame breaks, both riders are stuck, which is like a cluster built on one shared hard drive. The best idea: give each kid their own complete bicycle, keep both bikes rolling together in sync stride for stride, so if one bike's chain snaps mid-route, the other kid is already right there, already knows exactly where the route is, and can take over in seconds without missing a beat.

That's an Availability Group. Each SQL Server has its own complete, independent copy of the storage, kept in sync continuously, so if one server fails, the other one is already caught up and ready to take over immediately -- not eventually, and not from a shared drive that might be the very thing that failed.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The decision comes down to matching the mechanism to what actually broke at Brennan Manufacturing: a single storage-dependent server with no independent secondary copy of the data anywhere. Log shipping is ruled out first -- it ships transaction log backups to a secondary on an interval, which means the secondary is always some number of minutes behind, and failover is a manual, scripted process, not automatic. That reintroduces exactly the kind of data-loss window and manual-recovery delay that turned a hardware failure into a 48-hour outage. Database mirroring is ruled out even faster: it's a deprecated feature as of recent SQL Server versions, with Microsoft explicitly steering customers toward Availability Groups as its replacement, so building new infrastructure on it in this era would be choosing a feature already on its way out.

A Failover Cluster Instance (FCI) alone is the option worth taking seriously and still rejecting, because it genuinely solves half the problem: an FCI gives you automatic failover between nodes with no application changes needed, using the same Windows Server Failover Cluster mechanism as an AG. But a classic FCI relies on one shared storage array that both nodes attach to -- which means the database itself still has exactly one physical copy of its data files. That design protects against a server dying, but not against the storage array itself failing, which is uncomfortably close to the actual RAID-controller failure that started this whole engagement. An Availability Group solves that specific gap: `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` each own their own independent storage, `BrennanERP` is written to both under synchronous-commit availability mode inside `BrennanWSFC`, and `BrennanAGListener` gives applications one stable name to connect to regardless of which node is currently primary -- which is what makes the sub-60-second RTO from Lesson 2 achievable and testable, rather than theoretical. (This cluster-and-AG pattern is also one of the real skills this path is building toward DP-300, though the exam's current scope should always be checked against Microsoft's own official guidance rather than assumed from any one course.)

lessons.title: Designing the Two-Node Cluster and the Availability Group Topology
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding the real shape of BrennanWSFC and BrennanAG before touching a server -- how a two-node cluster gets quorum, why synchronous-commit with automatic failover is the right replication mode here, and why BrennanAGListener is the only name any application should ever be given.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The last lesson settled the stack: AlwaysOn Availability Groups, not failover clustered instances or log shipping, is how Brennan Manufacturing gets real high availability for `BrennanERP`. This lesson draws the actual topology that decision implies, in enough detail that nothing gets improvised later while a server is mid-build.

The shape is two Windows Servers, `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02`, joined into a Windows Server Failover Cluster named `BrennanWSFC`. On top of that cluster sits an Availability Group, `BrennanAG`, with `BrennanERP` as its first database. Applications never connect to `SQLDBA01` or `SQLDBA02` by name -- they connect to a single listener, `BrennanAGListener`, which always resolves to whichever node is currently primary. Three design questions have to be answered on the whiteboard before any of this is real: how does a *two*-node cluster get quorum when quorum is normally about majority vote, what replication mode makes failover actually automatic instead of just possible, and what exactly does the listener hide from the application layer. This lesson answers all three and leaves a decision record the next lessons build against.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of two people holding opposite ends of a rope, trying to vote on something. With only two voters, a tie is always possible -- there's no way to break it by just counting the two of them. So you bring in a third, neutral referee whose only job is to break ties. That referee doesn't do any of the real work; it just helps the two decide who's really in charge if they ever stop agreeing.

That's the first problem we solve here: `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` are our two rope-holders, and a small, cheap "referee" living in Azure -- a cloud witness -- is there only to break ties. Then we decide how fast the backup server has to copy every change (instantly, not "eventually"), and we give the whole system one single front door -- `BrennanAGListener` -- so nobody outside ever has to know or care which of the two servers is actually in charge today.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Windows Server Failover Clustering determines cluster health through quorum -- a vote among weighted voters that prevents split-brain by requiring a majority before the cluster will stay online. A two-node cluster with only the two node votes in play can produce an exact 50/50 split the moment one node is unreachable, which is precisely the ambiguous state quorum exists to prevent. The fix is a third vote that isn't a third server: a quorum witness. With `BrennanWSFC` already needing an Azure Storage dependency for off-site backups, a **cloud witness** backed by Azure Blob Storage is the right call over a file share witness -- no third on-prem server or site to maintain, and it survives a full outage of Brennan's physical location, which a file share witness hosted anywhere on that same site would not.

The second decision is the AG's availability mode. With exactly two replicas, `BrennanAG` is configured for **synchronous-commit** with **automatic failover** on both `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` -- every transaction committed on the primary is confirmed hardened on the secondary before the client gets its acknowledgment, which is what makes an automatic failover safe to allow without risking committed data the secondary never received. The tradeoff, and it has to be stated plainly in the design doc, is write latency: every commit now waits on a round trip to `SQLDBA02`, which is the cost of RPO-zero automatic failover and is why this pairing only makes sense when both nodes sit on a fast, reliable local network -- which they do.

The third piece is the listener. `BrennanAGListener` is a virtual network name with its own IP, registered in DNS, that always resolves to whichever replica currently holds the primary role. Every connection string Brennan's ERP application uses points at the listener, never at `SQLDBA01` or `SQLDBA02` directly -- that single fact is what makes a failover transparent to the application instead of an outage requiring a manual connection-string change.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name every piece before building anything

The whole topology, on paper:

```
            BrennanAGListener (VNN + static IP, port 1433)
                         |
        -----------------------------------
        |                                 |
   SQLDBA01 (primary)              SQLDBA02 (secondary)
   SQL Server instance              SQL Server instance
        |                                 |
        -----------------------------------
              Windows Server Failover Cluster
                     "BrennanWSFC"
                         |
              Cloud Witness (Azure Blob Storage,
              brennansqlbackups account, dedicated container)
                         |
              Availability Group "BrennanAG"
                databases: BrennanERP
```

Every name here is final. Nobody building a later lesson should need to invent an alternative.

## Step 2 -- Solve the two-node quorum problem

WSFC quorum requires a majority of weighted votes to keep the cluster online and prevent split-brain. With only `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` as node votes, a lost connection between them is a 1-1 tie -- unresolvable by the two nodes alone. A two-node WSFC always needs a third vote that is not a third SQL Server:

| Witness type | Where it lives | Fits Brennan? |
|---|---|---|
| File share witness | A plain SMB share on a third server | Needs a third on-prem server to maintain, and if it's on Brennan's site, a site-level event takes it out along with everything else |
| Cloud witness | An Azure Storage account, reachable over the internet | Independent of Brennan's site; already needs an Azure Storage account for off-site backups |

**Decision:** `BrennanWSFC` uses a **cloud witness** against the `brennansqlbackups` Azure Storage account, in a container dedicated to the witness blob and kept separate from the `offsite-backups` container used for database backups -- the two have different lifecycles and nobody should be able to accidentally apply a backup retention policy to the tie-breaking blob.

## Step 3 -- Choose the replication mode deliberately

AlwaysOn AG replicas run either asynchronous-commit (primary doesn't wait for the secondary, lower latency, but **manual** failover only -- data loss is possible) or synchronous-commit (primary waits for the secondary to harden the log, higher commit latency, but safe for **automatic** failover).

**Decision:** `BrennanAG` runs both `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` in **synchronous-commit** with **automatic failover** configured on both. With only two nodes on the same local network, the commit-latency cost is acceptable, and it buys the entire point of this project: a node failure recovers without a human being paged in the middle of the night.

## Step 4 -- Design the listener as the only front door

`BrennanAGListener` gets its own virtual network name and a dedicated static IP, registered in DNS, listening on port 1433. The ERP application's connection string is changed once, now, in planning, to target `BrennanAGListener` -- never `SQLDBA01` or `SQLDBA02` by hostname. That single rule is what makes a future failover invisible to the application layer: the listener always resolves to whichever node WSFC currently has marked primary, so the app reconnects to the same name and lands on the right server automatically.

## Step 5 -- Record what's explicitly out of scope for now

This design intentionally does not include: a third replica, a read-scale secondary, multi-subnet failover, or any database beyond `BrennanERP`. Keeping the first real AG small and provably correct matters more than covering every future need in the first design pass -- those are real conversations for later, not gaps in this one.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the topology: two-node BrennanWSFC with a cloud witness against the brennansqlbackups storage account (separate container from backups), BrennanAG running synchronous-commit with automatic failover on both SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02, and BrennanAGListener as the only endpoint the application will ever be configured against. No shared storage, no third replica, no read-scale secondary -- deliberately minimal and provably correct for BrennanERP before we touch a single server.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've finalized the blueprint for the new database cluster -- two servers, one shared 'front door' address the ERP system will always use, and a lightweight tie-breaker hosted in Azure so the cluster can make decisions on its own if one server goes down. Nothing gets built yet; this is the design everyone signs off on before infrastructure work starts next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've finished designing the resilience architecture for the ERP database -- two servers working as a pair, with instant, automatic handoff if one fails, and no changes required to how the ERP application connects. Construction of the actual cluster begins in the next phase.

lessons.title: Planning the Backup Strategy, Including an Azure Off-Site Copy
lessons.summary: A real cadence for full, differential, and log backups of BrennanERP, where those backups should run on an AG, and why a genuine off-site copy in Azure Storage is still required even after the cluster goes live.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`BrennanAG` protects `BrennanERP` against a *node* failing -- `SQLDBA01` going down, a Windows Update reboot, a disk controller dying. It does nothing for a *site*-level event: a fire, a ransomware attack that encrypts both nodes because they share the same network, or a mistake that drops a table on the primary and instantly replicates onto the secondary. Backups are still the only real protection against those, and this lesson plans exactly how they work: the cadence of full, differential, and transaction log backups for `BrennanERP`, which replica actually runs them, how long they're kept, and how a true off-site copy lands in Azure so Brennan isn't one building away from losing everything.

Nothing gets scripted yet. This lesson produces the backup plan the automation lessons later in this series build against, using the real `dbatools` PowerShell toolkit and SQL Server's native backup-to-URL feature.
lessons.explainSimple: Having two servers that back each other up is like having two copies of an important document in the same filing cabinet -- great protection if one copy gets coffee spilled on it, useless if the whole cabinet burns down. So on top of the two-server setup, we still need a real backup plan: a full copy on a schedule, smaller daily copies of just what changed, and a mailed-off photocopy that lives somewhere else entirely -- in this case, a storage account in Azure, far away from Brennan's building.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Treating AlwaysOn AG as a backup strategy is a common and costly mistake -- synchronous replication propagates both intended writes and mistakes with equal fidelity, and it does nothing for a fire, a stolen building, or ransomware that spreads across a flat local network. `BrennanERP` needs a conventional, independent backup cadence regardless of the AG: a **weekly full**, **daily differential**, and a **transaction log backup every 15 minutes** -- the log interval set by Brennan's tolerance for data loss (RPO), not by convenience.

An AG also changes *where* backups should run. SQL Server's **backup preference** setting on the availability group (`Prefer Secondary`, in this case) lets automated jobs query `sys.fn_hadr_backup_is_preferred_replica` and run full/differential backups against `SQLDBA02` instead of the primary, offloading that I/O from the node actually serving the ERP application -- with the caveat that a full or differential backup taken on a secondary is always `COPY_ONLY`, since a secondary can't participate in a differential backup chain the way a primary can.

The off-site piece is SQL Server's native **backup-to-URL**: writing the backup file directly to a container in Azure Blob Storage rather than a local or SAN path, authenticated with a SQL Server `CREDENTIAL` built from a Shared Access Signature -- never the full storage account key, which is broader access than a backup job needs. That lands every backup in the `offsite-backups` container of the `brennansqlbackups` storage account, genuinely outside Brennan's building, which is the one thing the AG itself can never provide.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State plainly what the AG does not cover

`BrennanAG`'s synchronous replication protects against a node failing. It provides **zero** protection against: a dropped table or bad `UPDATE` (replicated instantly to the secondary), ransomware spreading across both nodes on the same network, or a fire, flood, or theft affecting Brennan's one physical site. Backups remain mandatory with the AG in place, not optional.

## Step 2 -- Set the backup cadence for BrennanERP

| Backup type | Cadence | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Full | Weekly | Baseline for every restore chain |
| Differential | Daily | Keeps restore time reasonable without a full backup every night |
| Transaction log | Every 15 minutes | Caps data loss (RPO) at 15 minutes in a true disaster, independent of the AG |

## Step 3 -- Decide which replica actually runs the backups

`BrennanAG`'s backup preference is set to **Prefer Secondary**, so scheduled jobs check `sys.fn_hadr_backup_is_preferred_replica` and run full and differential backups against `SQLDBA02`, keeping that I/O off the node actively serving the ERP application. Two rules that follow from this:

- Full/differential backups taken on the secondary must be marked `COPY_ONLY` -- a secondary can't anchor a real differential base.
- Transaction log backups still have to run reliably regardless of which node is currently primary after a failover, so the job logic checks replica role every run rather than assuming `SQLDBA02` is always secondary.

## Step 4 -- Design the off-site copy via backup-to-URL

```sql
-- Planned: a database-scoped credential backed by a SAS token,
-- not the full storage account key
CREATE CREDENTIAL [https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups]
    WITH IDENTITY = 'SHARED ACCESS SIGNATURE',
    SECRET = '<SAS token, scoped to this container, write + create only>';

-- Planned shape of the backup statement itself
BACKUP DATABASE [BrennanERP]
TO URL = 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups/BrennanERP_full.bak'
WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM;
```

The SAS token is scoped only to the `offsite-backups` container, with write and create permissions and an expiry, rather than the account key -- a leaked backup credential should not be able to read or delete anything else in the storage account.

## Step 5 -- Set retention, on both sides

Local backups (on `SQLDBA02`'s disk, before upload) are kept 7 days as a fast-restore buffer. The off-site copy in `offsite-backups` is retained 35 days online, with Azure Blob lifecycle management configured to move anything older than 35 days to cool-tier storage automatically rather than deleting it outright -- cheaper, without needing a second manual cleanup job.

## Step 6 -- Plan how this gets verified, not just scheduled

A backup nobody has ever restored is a theory, not a plan. The automation lessons later in this series will use `dbatools`' `Backup-DbaDatabase` to run the jobs above and `Test-DbaLastBackup` to automatically restore the most recent backup to a scratch instance and run `DBCC CHECKDB` against it on a schedule -- so a corrupt or unusable backup is caught within a day, not discovered during a real disaster.

## Step 7 -- Decide who finds out when a backup job fails

A backup plan with no failure alerting is indistinguishable from no backup plan at all until the day it's needed. Every scheduled job in this design -- the weekly full, the daily differential, the 15-minute log backups, and the nightly `Test-DbaLastBackup` restore check -- is planned to raise a SQL Server Agent alert on failure, routed to an operator mailbox the DBA team actually watches, the same day the failure happens rather than surfacing at a quarterly audit.

## Step 8 -- Write down the restore order, before it's ever needed under pressure

The last piece of this plan is the restore sequence itself, written out now while nobody is in a hurry: most recent full, then the most recent differential taken after that full, then every transaction log backup taken since, applied in order with `NORECOVERY` until the final one, which is applied `WITH RECOVERY`. Having this sequence already documented turns a real disaster into a checklist instead of a conversation.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Backup plan for BrennanERP: weekly full, daily differential, log backups every 15 minutes, with full/differential running against SQLDBA02 under a Prefer Secondary AG backup preference (marked COPY_ONLY accordingly). Off-site copy lands in the offsite-backups container of brennansqlbackups via native backup-to-URL, authenticated with a container-scoped SAS credential rather than the account key. 7-day local retention, 35-day off-site retention with lifecycle tiering after that. Restore verification via dbatools Test-DbaLastBackup is planned, not optional.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Even with the new two-server cluster, we still need real backups -- the cluster protects against a server failing, not against a fire, theft, or a mistake that gets copied to both servers instantly. We've planned a full weekly backup, smaller daily backups, and frequent small backups throughout the day, all shipped off-site to a secure cloud location Brennan's building failing wouldn't affect.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've planned a genuine backup strategy for the ERP database that's independent of the new resilient server pair -- including an automatic copy stored off-site in the cloud, so a site-level event like a fire can't take down both the live system and its backups at once. We're also planning to regularly test restoring from these backups, not just assume they'll work when needed.

lessons.title: Planning the Performance Baseline and Monitoring Approach
lessons.summary: What to capture before any tuning work starts -- wait stats and top resource-consuming queries on BrennanERP -- plus the ongoing monitoring of AG health, Agent jobs, and disk/CPU that keeps this from being a one-time exercise.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Once `BrennanWSFC` and `BrennanAG` exist, Brennan's team is going to want to know two different things over time: "is the database actually fast," and "is the resilience we just built still healthy." Both questions are unanswerable without a reference point captured *before* anything changes -- and both need an ongoing monitoring layer, not a one-time health check that nobody repeats. This lesson plans both: a performance baseline for `BrennanERP` captured now, before the AG exists and again right after, and a standing monitoring plan that watches AG health, SQL Server Agent job outcomes, and basic infrastructure counters for the life of the system.

No tuning happens in this lesson. The point is capturing the "before" picture and designing the ongoing watch -- the tuning work itself belongs to the dedicated performance-tuning course this series is demonstrating, not this plan.
lessons.explainSimple: You can't tell if a car got slower after a repair if you never timed it before the repair. Before we touch anything, we're going to write down exactly how the database behaves today -- which parts of it are waiting on what, and which specific tasks take the most effort. Then, after the new servers go live, we check the same measurements again. And instead of checking just once and walking away, we set up something that keeps watching every day, so a new problem gets noticed in hours, not months.
lessons.explainProfessional:
"The database feels slow" is not an actionable finding without a baseline to compare against, and capturing that baseline has two real components. The first is **wait statistics** -- `sys.dm_os_wait_stats` accumulates, cluster-wide, every time a worker thread had to wait and why, and clearing it with `DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR)` before a known observation window turns it into a snapshot of exactly what `BrennanERP` spent its time waiting on: disk I/O, locking, CPU scheduling, or -- after the AG exists -- `HADR_SYNC_COMMIT`, the wait that directly reflects the latency cost from Lesson 5's synchronous-commit decision. The second is a **top resource-consumer baseline**: Query Store, enabled on `BrennanERP`, captures execution plans and runtime stats per query so the heaviest CPU, duration, and logical-read consumers over a representative window are known by name, not guessed at.

The AG changes this in one important way: the wait-stats and Query Store baseline has to be captured **twice** -- once before the AG exists, and once again shortly after cutover -- because synchronous commit genuinely adds latency, and the team needs to know, in writing, exactly how much, rather than discovering it informally the first time someone complains the ERP system "feels different."

A baseline captured once and never revisited is a one-time exercise, not monitoring. The standing plan layers three things on top: SQL Server Agent job-outcome alerting (a failed backup or maintenance job surfaces same-day, not at the next audit), AG health monitoring via `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states` and the Always On dashboard (catching a replica silently falling behind on synchronization before it becomes a failed failover), and basic infrastructure thresholds on disk space and CPU on both `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02`.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Decide what "baseline" actually means here

Two captures, not one: a pre-AG baseline of `BrennanERP` on its current single server, and a post-cutover baseline taken shortly after `BrennanAG` goes live. The gap between the two is the honest, measured cost of synchronous-commit replication -- a number the team will need the first time anyone asks why a report feels slower.

## Step 2 -- Plan the wait-stats capture

```sql
-- Planned capture procedure, run at the start of a defined window
DBCC SQLPERF('sys.dm_os_wait_stats', CLEAR);

-- ... representative workload runs for the observation window ...

SELECT TOP 20
    wait_type,
    wait_time_ms,
    waiting_tasks_count,
    signal_wait_time_ms
FROM sys.dm_os_wait_stats
WHERE wait_type NOT IN ('SLEEP_TASK','BROKER_TASK_STOP') -- exclude known benign waits
ORDER BY wait_time_ms DESC;
```

The pre-AG run should show mostly disk-I/O and CPU-scheduling waits. The post-cutover run is expected to show a new, meaningful `HADR_SYNC_COMMIT` entry -- that's not a problem to fix, it's the AG's design cost being measured instead of assumed.

## Step 3 -- Plan the top-resource-consumer capture

Query Store gets enabled on `BrennanERP` ahead of the observation window:

```sql
ALTER DATABASE [BrennanERP] SET QUERY_STORE = ON;
ALTER DATABASE [BrennanERP] SET QUERY_STORE (OPERATION_MODE = READ_WRITE);
```

After a representative business day, the top 10 queries by total CPU, by total duration, and by total logical reads are pulled from the Query Store views and recorded by name and object -- this list becomes the literal input to the dedicated performance-tuning work later in this series, not a separate guess.

## Step 4 -- Capture an infrastructure baseline alongside the SQL-level one

Using `dbatools`:

```powershell
Get-DbaDiskSpace -ComputerName SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02
Get-DbaCpuUsage -ComputerName SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02
Get-DbaWaitStatistic -SqlInstance SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 -Threshold 5
```

Recorded once now, and again post-cutover, as the plain infrastructure half of the same comparison.

## Step 5 -- Design the standing monitoring layer

Three watch areas, each with a named owner once built:

- **Agent job outcomes** -- every backup, log-shipping (pre-AG), and maintenance job alerts on failure the same day, not discovered at a later audit.
- **AG health** -- `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states.synchronization_health` checked on a schedule; a replica stuck at `NOT HEALTHY` or `PARTIALLY_HEALTHY` for more than a few minutes pages someone, because a silently unhealthy secondary is a failover that will not actually succeed when needed.
- **Disk and CPU thresholds** on both `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02`, since a full disk on either node threatens the whole AG, not just whichever one happens to be primary that day.

## Step 6 -- Record where this baseline gets used next

This baseline is the literal starting input for two things later in Brennan's roadmap: the dedicated performance-tuning work that follows this series, and any future troubleshooting lesson that needs to answer "was it always like this, or did something change" with evidence instead of memory.

## Step 7 -- Decide how long raw baseline data is kept

Wait-stats snapshots and Query Store history are only useful for comparison if they're still around months later when someone actually needs them. The plan keeps 90 days of Query Store history on `BrennanERP` (`QUERY_CAPTURE_MODE = AUTO` to avoid capturing every trivial one-off query) and exports both the pre-AG and post-cutover wait-stats snapshots to a plain results table outside `sys.dm_os_wait_stats`, since that view resets on every SQL Server service restart and would otherwise quietly lose the exact "before" picture this whole lesson exists to protect.

## Step 8 -- Name who owns the ongoing watch

A monitoring plan with no named owner decays into dashboards nobody opens. Agent job alerting, AG health checks, and the disk/CPU thresholds are each assigned to the on-call DBA rotation once built, with a documented escalation path if an alert goes unacknowledged -- turning this from a one-time baseline exercise into the standing discipline it's meant to be.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned a two-point performance baseline for BrennanERP -- wait stats via sys.dm_os_wait_stats and top Query Store consumers, captured once before the AG exists and again right after cutover, specifically to measure the real HADR_SYNC_COMMIT cost rather than guess at it. Standing monitoring layered on top: Agent job failure alerting, AG health via sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, and disk/CPU thresholds on both nodes. No tuning in this lesson -- this is the reference data the tuning work and future troubleshooting both depend on.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Before we flip on the new resilient setup, we're recording exactly how the database performs today, so we have real numbers to compare against afterward instead of relying on anyone's impression that 'it feels different.' We're also setting up ongoing automatic checks -- failed backup jobs, cluster health, disk space -- so a new problem gets caught within a day rather than during the next audit.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're establishing a measured 'before' picture of database performance so we can prove, with numbers, whether the new reliability investment has any performance tradeoff -- rather than relying on anecdotes later. We're also putting ongoing automated monitoring in place so small problems get caught early, before they become the kind of outage that started this project.

lessons.title: Building the Windows Server Failover Cluster
lessons.summary: Standing up BrennanWSFC for real -- the Failover Clustering feature on both nodes, cluster validation, cluster creation without shared storage, and a cloud witness against Azure Storage -- turning three lessons of planning into the first real infrastructure.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Three lessons of planning end here. This is the first lesson in the series where real infrastructure gets created: the Windows Server Failover Cluster, `BrennanWSFC`, spanning `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02`, with the cloud witness designed in Lesson 5 actually configured against the `brennansqlbackups` Azure Storage account.

This lesson does not yet create `BrennanAG` or touch `BrennanERP` -- the Availability Group is built on top of this cluster in a later lesson, once the cluster itself is validated and healthy. What matters here is that every step traces directly back to a decision already made: no shared disk (the AG doesn't need one), a cloud witness and not a file share witness, and a static cluster IP sized for exactly two nodes.
lessons.explainSimple: If Lesson 5 was the blueprint, this is the day the foundation actually gets poured. We turn on the clustering feature on both servers, run a real inspection to make sure they're actually compatible with each other, join them together under one cluster name, and then connect the referee we designed -- a small storage location in Azure -- so the cluster can always break a tie on its own. By the end of this lesson, `BrennanWSFC` is a real, running cluster. The database-specific piece on top of it is still to come.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Cluster validation is not an optional courtesy step -- `Test-Cluster` runs the same network, storage, and system-configuration checks Microsoft support will ask for first if this cluster is ever opened as a support case, and running it *before* cluster creation catches a networking or AD mismatch while it's still a five-minute fix instead of a production incident. Because `BrennanAG` uses AlwaysOn's own log-based replication rather than shared storage, cluster creation is explicitly run without a disk witness or shared volume -- the only shared dependency this cluster has is the cloud witness itself, configured directly against Blob Storage using a storage account access key scoped to that purpose.

Once `New-Cluster` returns, the cluster is live but not yet proven under the exact failure condition it exists for -- a quorum check and witness verification close this lesson instead of trusting the happy path of `New-Cluster` completing without error.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm prerequisites on both nodes

```powershell
# Run from a management workstation with RSAT installed
Test-Connection -ComputerName SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02
Get-ADComputer -Identity SQLDBA01
Get-ADComputer -Identity SQLDBA02
```

Both nodes must already be domain-joined, on the same OS build, and reachable on the network Brennan's team dedicated to cluster traffic -- any mismatch here fails validation in Step 3 anyway, so it's worth confirming before installing anything.

## Step 2 -- Install the Failover Clustering feature on both nodes

```powershell
Invoke-Command -ComputerName SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 -ScriptBlock {
    Install-WindowsFeature -Name Failover-Clustering -IncludeManagementTools
}
```

`-IncludeManagementTools` pulls in Failover Cluster Manager and the PowerShell module used for every remaining step -- skip it and the cmdlets below aren't available locally on either node.

## Step 3 -- Validate before creating anything

```powershell
Test-Cluster -Node SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 `
    -Include "Inventory", "Network", "System Configuration"
```

This produces an HTML report under `C:\Windows\Cluster\Reports` on the node it ran from. Review it line by line -- specifically the network adapter and Active Directory checks -- before moving on. A validation warning here is cheaper to fix now than after the cluster exists.

## Step 4 -- Create the cluster, with no shared storage

```powershell
New-Cluster -Name BrennanWSFC `
    -Node SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 `
    -StaticAddress 10.20.4.50 `
    -NoStorage
```

`-NoStorage` is deliberate, not an oversight: `BrennanAG` replicates via log shipment inside SQL Server, not shared disk, so this cluster has no shared volume to validate or own. The static address becomes the cluster's own management IP, separate from the `BrennanAGListener` IP that gets configured when the Availability Group itself is built.

## Step 5 -- Configure the cloud witness against Azure Storage

```powershell
Set-ClusterQuorum -CloudWitness `
    -AccountName brennansqlbackups `
    -AccessKey "<storage-account-access-key>"
```

This points `BrennanWSFC`'s quorum witness at the `brennansqlbackups` storage account, in the dedicated witness container planned in Lesson 5 -- kept separate from the `offsite-backups` container that will hold actual database backups, so the two lifecycles never collide.

## Step 6 -- Verify the cluster is actually healthy, not just created

```powershell
Get-Cluster | Select-Object Name, QuorumType
Get-ClusterNode
Test-Cluster -Node SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 -Include "Inventory", "Network", "System Configuration"
```

Confirm `QuorumType` reports `CloudWitness`, both nodes show `State = Up` under `Get-ClusterNode`, and the post-creation validation report comes back clean. This is the point to deliberately take `SQLDBA02` offline briefly and confirm the cluster stays quorate on `SQLDBA01` alone with the witness vote -- proving the two-node quorum design from Lesson 5 actually holds before anything depends on it.

## Step 7 -- What's deliberately not done yet

`BrennanWSFC` exists, is validated, and is quorate. `BrennanAG` and `BrennanERP` are not touched in this lesson -- the Availability Group gets built on top of this now-proven cluster next, so any AG-level issue in that lesson can be diagnosed knowing the cluster underneath it is already sound.

## Step 8 -- Document the cluster's own network and account footprint

Before moving on, the cluster's management IP, the cloud witness account and container, and the domain account used to create the cluster all get written into Brennan's infrastructure documentation -- not left to be reverse-engineered later from Failover Cluster Manager by whoever next needs to touch this. `Get-ClusterResource` and `Get-ClusterNetwork` are run one more time specifically to capture this record:

```powershell
Get-ClusterResource | Select-Object Name, State, OwnerGroup
Get-ClusterNetwork | Select-Object Name, Address, State
```

This closes the loop started back in Lesson 5: every name and setting on the whiteboard now has a corresponding real object that's been verified, documented, and proven to survive a node going offline.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: BrennanWSFC is live: Failover-Clustering installed on both SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02, cluster validated clean before and after creation, created with -NoStorage since the AG needs no shared disk, and quorum backed by a cloud witness against the brennansqlbackups storage account in its own dedicated container. Took SQLDBA02 offline briefly post-build and confirmed the cluster stayed quorate on SQLDBA01 alone -- the two-node quorum design holds. BrennanAG itself is next, built on top of this now-proven cluster.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The two servers are now officially joined together as a cluster, and we've verified it can correctly handle one server going offline without losing track of what's happening -- using a small tie-breaking service in Azure instead of a third physical server. This is real, running infrastructure, not a diagram anymore. The database-specific resilience layer goes on top of this next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The foundation of the new resilient server pair is now physically built and tested -- we deliberately took one server offline during testing to confirm the system handles that correctly, and it did. The next step adds the database-level protection on top of this proven foundation.

lessons.title: Creating the AlwaysOn Availability Group and Listener
lessons.summary: The centerpiece of Brennan's high-availability build: standing up BrennanAG across SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 on top of the BrennanWSFC cluster, with BrennanERP as its first database and a stable listener endpoint for client connections.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the Windows Server Failover Cluster **BrennanWSFC** already built across **SQLDBA01** (primary) and **SQLDBA02** (secondary), this lesson creates the actual high-availability mechanism that sits on top of it: an AlwaysOn Availability Group named **BrennanAG**.

BrennanAG starts with exactly one database in it — **BrennanERP**, Brennan Manufacturing's core ERP database — configured for synchronous-commit, automatic failover between the two replicas. On top of that we create **BrennanAGListener**, the single stable network name and IP address every application and reporting tool will use to reach BrennanERP, regardless of which of the two servers currently holds the primary role.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think of BrennanAG like a two-person relay team where both people are holding the exact same baton at the exact same time, not passing it back and forth. **SQLDBA01** and **SQLDBA02** both keep an up-to-the-second copy of the **BrennanERP** database. If SQLDBA01 ever falls over, SQLDBA02 already has everything and can take over automatically, almost instantly.

The listener, **BrennanAGListener**, is like a single phone number that always rings whichever person is "it" right now. Nobody calling in ever needs to know or care which of the two servers is actually answering — they just dial the one number.
lessons.explainProfessional:
BrennanAG is configured with synchronous-commit availability mode and automatic failover mode between SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 — the combination that gives Brennan an actual zero-data-loss automatic failover, not just a replicated copy that still requires a human to flip a switch. That combination only works because both replicas sit inside the same Windows Server Failover Cluster, BrennanWSFC, which supplies the quorum and health-detection logic the Availability Group relies on for failover decisions.

BrennanERP is added to the Availability Group at creation time, which is the easy case. The detail worth internalizing now, because it matters again later in this project: adding any *additional* database to BrennanAG after today is never automatic just because a server already participates in the AG. It is always a deliberate, two-step operation — seed the new database onto the secondary from a real backup, then explicitly alter the Availability Group to add it. A database that simply exists on SQLDBA01 is not inside BrennanAG until someone performs that two-step process by hand.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Confirm prerequisites before touching the Availability Group

BrennanWSFC is already built across SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02, the AlwaysOn Availability Groups feature is enabled in SQL Server Configuration Manager on both instances, and BrennanERP is already running in FULL recovery model with a current full backup. Confirm the recovery model from SQLDBA01:

```sql
SELECT name, recovery_model_desc
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = 'BrennanERP';
```

## Step 2 — Create the Availability Group on SQLDBA01

Run this on the primary, SQLDBA01. It defines both replicas, their endpoint URLs, and the availability/failover behavior, and adds BrennanERP as the Availability Group's first database:

```sql
CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG
WITH (AUTOMATED_BACKUP_PREFERENCE = SECONDARY)
FOR DATABASE BrennanERP
REPLICA ON
    'SQLDBA01' WITH (
        ENDPOINT_URL = 'TCP://SQLDBA01.brennan.local:5022',
        AVAILABILITY_MODE = SYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT,
        FAILOVER_MODE = AUTOMATIC,
        SECONDARY_ROLE (ALLOW_CONNECTIONS = NO)
    ),
    'SQLDBA02' WITH (
        ENDPOINT_URL = 'TCP://SQLDBA02.brennan.local:5022',
        AVAILABILITY_MODE = SYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT,
        FAILOVER_MODE = AUTOMATIC,
        SECONDARY_ROLE (ALLOW_CONNECTIONS = NO)
    );
```

## Step 3 — Join SQLDBA02 and seed BrennanERP onto it

On SQLDBA02, join the Availability Group, then restore BrennanERP from the primary's full and log backups WITH NORECOVERY so the secondary has a matching starting point before it joins the data movement:

```sql
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG JOIN;
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG GRANT CREATE ANY DATABASE;

RESTORE DATABASE BrennanERP
FROM DISK = N'\\SQLDBA01\Backups\BrennanERP_Full.bak'
WITH NORECOVERY, REPLACE;

RESTORE LOG BrennanERP
FROM DISK = N'\\SQLDBA01\Backups\BrennanERP_Log.trn'
WITH NORECOVERY;

ALTER DATABASE BrennanERP SET HADR AVAILABILITY GROUP = BrennanAG;
```

Confirm both replicas are synchronized back on SQLDBA01:

```sql
SELECT ar.replica_server_name, drs.synchronization_state_desc, drs.is_suspended
FROM sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states drs
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON drs.replica_id = ar.replica_id;
```

## Step 4 — Create the listener, BrennanAGListener

Still on SQLDBA01, give the Availability Group its single stable connection point:

```sql
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG
ADD LISTENER 'BrennanAGListener' (
    WITH IP ((N'10.50.12.60', N'255.255.255.0')),
    PORT = 1433
);
```

Every connection string going forward — the ERP application, SSRS, any ad hoc reporting tool — points at `BrennanAGListener`, never at `SQLDBA01` or `SQLDBA02` by name. That's what makes the eventual failover invisible to anything connecting to BrennanERP.

## Step 5 — The one dbatools shortcut worth knowing

Everything above can also be done in a single dbatools call, which is useful for documenting the build or repeating it in a lab environment — New-DbaAvailabilityGroup wraps the create, join, seed, and listener creation into one cmdlet:

```powershell
New-DbaAvailabilityGroup -Primary SQLDBA01 -Secondary SQLDBA02 `
    -Name BrennanAG -Database BrennanERP `
    -ClusterType Wsfc -AvailabilityMode SynchronousCommit -FailoverMode Automatic `
    -SeedingMode Automatic -IPAddress 10.50.12.60 -SubnetMask 255.255.255.0 `
    -Port 1433 -Confirm:$false
```

Whichever path builds it, BrennanAG today contains exactly one database: BrennanERP. That's a fact worth stating plainly, because it is not self-updating — any database created on SQLDBA01 later sits outside BrennanAG until it is deliberately backed up, restored to SQLDBA02, and added to the group with `ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG ADD DATABASE <name>`. Being on a clustered, AlwaysOn-enabled server does not put a database inside the Availability Group by itself.

## Step 6 — Confirm the listener actually resolves and routes correctly

Before calling this done, verify from a client machine, not just from SQLDBA01 itself, that the listener name resolves and routes to whichever replica currently holds the primary role:

```powershell
Resolve-DnsName -Name BrennanAGListener.brennan.local
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName BrennanAGListener.brennan.local -Port 1433
```

And from SQL Server directly, confirm which replica BrennanAGListener is currently routing to, plus the overall health of the Availability Group:

```sql
SELECT ag.name AS ag_name, ar.replica_server_name, ars.role_desc, ars.synchronization_health_desc
FROM sys.availability_groups ag
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON ag.group_id = ar.group_id
JOIN sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states ars ON ar.replica_id = ars.replica_id;
```

`synchronization_health_desc` should read `HEALTHY` for both SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 before this build is considered finished — not just "no errors in the SQL Server error log," but an explicit, queried confirmation.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: BrennanAG is live across SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 on top of BrennanWSFC — synchronous-commit, automatic failover, both replicas confirmed SYNCHRONIZED. BrennanERP is the only database in the group right now. Listener is BrennanAGListener on 10.50.12.60:1433; I've pointed the ERP app's connection string at the listener name, not either server name directly. One thing to flag for the backlog: any new database we stand up later does not join BrennanAG automatically — that's always a manual backup/restore/ADD DATABASE step, so we need a checklist item for it whenever a new database goes to production.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The core high-availability piece is in place: if SQLDBA01 has a problem, SQLDBA02 takes over automatically with no data loss and no application changes, because everything connects through one stable address instead of a specific server name. Right now this protection covers BrennanERP, the main ERP database. It's worth noting that any future database we add to the server doesn't get this protection automatically — it has to be deliberately added, which is a step we'll want in our standard rollout checklist.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our core business system now has real built-in protection against a server failure — if the main server goes down, a second server takes over automatically within seconds, with no data lost and no action needed from staff. This protection is active today for our ERP database.

lessons.title: Automating Backups and Maintenance With PowerShell
lessons.summary: Turning backups and index/statistics upkeep into unattended, verified PowerShell automation with the dbatools toolkit, scheduled through SQL Server Agent instead of relying on anyone remembering to run a script.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: An Availability Group protects BrennanERP from a server failing. It does nothing to protect against a bad deployment, a mistaken DELETE, or ordinary index and statistics drift that slowly makes queries slower over months. This lesson builds that second layer of protection: a scheduled, unattended PowerShell automation built on the **dbatools** toolkit that takes real backups, actually proves those backups can be restored, and keeps indexes and statistics healthy — all without anyone having to remember to run anything.
lessons.explainSimple: Taking a backup is like putting a spare key under a flowerpot. That's only useful if the key actually opens the door — if nobody ever checks, you might discover on the worst possible day that the key was bent the whole time. This lesson does two things: it makes a fresh spare key automatically, on a schedule, and it automatically tries that key in the lock every so often to prove it still works, long before anyone actually needs it.
lessons.explainProfessional: Three dbatools cmdlets carry this lesson: Backup-DbaDatabase for the actual full and log backups, Test-DbaLastBackup for restore verification, and Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance for index and statistics upkeep. The ordering matters as much as the cmdlets themselves — a backup that has never been test-restored is a backup you are merely hoping works, and a maintenance job that rebuilds indexes without ever checking integrity is optimizing a database you haven't confirmed is actually sound. Wrapping all three in scheduled SQL Server Agent jobs, rather than a script someone has to remember to kick off, is what turns "we have backups" into a fact you can actually rely on at 2am.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Full and log backups with Backup-DbaDatabase

On SQLDBA01, a full backup runs nightly and log backups run every fifteen minutes, both landing in a local backup share before lesson 12 adds an off-site copy:

```powershell
# Nightly full backup
Backup-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database BrennanERP `
    -Type Full -Path '\\SQLDBA01\Backups\Full' `
    -CompressBackup -Checksum -Verify

# Log backup, every 15 minutes
Backup-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database BrennanERP `
    -Type Log -Path '\\SQLDBA01\Backups\Log' `
    -CompressBackup -Checksum
```

`-Checksum` and `-Verify` catch a corrupt backup file at creation time rather than letting it sit untouched until the day someone actually needs it.

## Step 2 — Prove the backup is actually restorable

A backup file existing on disk is not the same claim as a backup being restorable. Test-DbaLastBackup takes the most recent backup, performs a real restore to a scratch location, runs DBCC CHECKDB against the restored copy, and then drops it:

```powershell
Test-DbaLastBackup -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database BrennanERP `
    -Destination SQLDBA02 `
    -DataDirectory 'D:\DBATools\TestRestore\Data' `
    -LogDirectory 'D:\DBATools\TestRestore\Log' |
    Select-Object SourceServer, Database, RestoreResult, DbccResult
```
