A result of `RestoreResult = Success` and `DbccResult = Success` is the actual evidence a backup is usable — not an assumption based on file size or a job that reported "completed."

## Step 3 — Keep indexes and statistics healthy with Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance

AlwaysOn and backups protect availability and recoverability; they don't stop ordinary index fragmentation and stale statistics from degrading query performance over time. Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance handles that upkeep directly against BrennanERP on a weekly maintenance window:

```powershell
Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database BrennanERP `
    -Type Index, Statistics -LogToTable
```

`-LogToTable` keeps a running history of what was rebuilt or reorganized each week, which matters the first time someone asks whether a slow query is connected to maintenance that didn't run.

## Step 4 — Schedule it through SQL Server Agent, not a person's memory

Each PowerShell step becomes its own SQL Server Agent job step, calling `powershell.exe` against a saved `.ps1` script so none of this depends on anyone being online to kick it off:

```powershell
New-DbaAgentJob -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Job 'BrennanERP - Full Backup' `
    -Description 'Nightly full backup via dbatools, verified with checksum'

New-DbaAgentJobStep -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Job 'BrennanERP - Full Backup' `
    -StepName 'Run Backup-DbaDatabase' -Subsystem CmdExec `
    -Command 'powershell.exe -File D:\Scripts\Backup-BrennanERP-Full.ps1'

New-DbaAgentSchedule -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Job 'BrennanERP - Full Backup' `
    -Schedule 'Nightly-0200' -FrequencyType Daily -FrequencyInterval 1 `
    -StartTime 020000
```

The same pattern repeats for the log-backup job (every 15 minutes), the Test-DbaLastBackup verification job (weekly), and the Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance job (weekly, outside business hours).

## Step 5 — Clean up old backup files so the share doesn't fill up silently

An automated backup job that never prunes its own output eventually fails for the least useful possible reason — a full disk. dbatools' own cleanup cmdlet runs as a fifth scheduled step, removing backup files older than Brennan's 14-day local retention window:

```powershell
Remove-DbaBackup -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -BackupFileExtension bak,trn `
    -Path '\\SQLDBA01\Backups' -CheckArchiveBit -RetentionPeriod 14d
```

## Step 6 — Review job history, not just job status

"The job succeeded" and "the backup is good" are two different claims. Reviewing Agent job history alongside the Test-DbaLastBackup log table is the weekly habit that catches a quietly degrading job — one that completes every night but has started silently skipping the checksum step, for example — before it becomes a real incident:

```powershell
Get-DbaAgentJobHistory -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Job 'BrennanERP - Full Backup' -Since (Get-Date).AddDays(-7) |
    Select-Object RunDate, RunStatus, RunDuration
```

With these six pieces running on their own schedule, BrennanERP has a backup chain that is automated, space-managed, and — because of Step 2 — actually proven restorable, not just assumed to be.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Backups on SQLDBA01 are fully automated through dbatools: nightly full and 15-minute log backups via Backup-DbaDatabase with checksum verification, a weekly Test-DbaLastBackup job that actually restores and DBCC-checks the latest backup rather than trusting the file exists, and a weekly Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance pass for index and statistics health. All four run as scheduled SQL Server Agent jobs, not manual scripts, with Remove-DbaBackup pruning old files and job history reviewed weekly so a quietly degrading job gets caught instead of discovered during a real incident.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Database backups and routine maintenance for the ERP system are now fully automated and self-checking — the system doesn't just take backups, it actually tests that they can be restored on a regular schedule, which is the part most companies skip. This removes a recurring manual task from the DBA's plate and closes a real risk: a backup nobody has ever actually tried restoring.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our financial and operational data is now being backed up automatically every night, and — just as importantly — the system automatically proves those backups actually work by restoring them on a schedule, instead of us finding out the hard way during an emergency.

lessons.title: Tuning a Real Slow Query With Execution Plans and Missing Indexes
lessons.summary: A real production-floor report query is timing out schedulers. We capture its actual execution plan, pull SQL Server's own missing-index recommendation, and validate a real CREATE INDEX statement with a measured before/after duration.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Production supervisors on Brennan's shop floor have started complaining that the daily work-order status report, run against **BrennanERP**, takes almost a full minute to load — long enough that people have started avoiding it. This lesson diagnoses that complaint the right way: capture the query's actual execution plan, read what SQL Server itself is recommending, and apply and verify a real index fix with a measured before-and-after duration, instead of guessing.
lessons.explainSimple: Imagine looking for one specific book in a library that has no card catalog — you'd have to walk down every single aisle and check every shelf. An index is the card catalog: it tells the database exactly which aisle and shelf to go to. This lesson finds a report that's slow because the database is still "walking every aisle," builds the right card catalog entry for it, and then times the search both before and after to prove the fix actually worked.
lessons.explainProfessional: The temptation with a slow query is to add an index based on intuition about which columns "should" help. This lesson deliberately doesn't do that — it captures the actual execution plan, reads SQL Server's own missing-index DMVs for a concrete, cost-ranked recommendation, and only then writes the CREATE INDEX statement, naming it explicitly rather than accepting the system-generated name. The before/after duration comparison at the end is the part that's easy to skip under time pressure and is also the only part that actually proves the fix worked rather than just looks plausible.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Reproduce the slow query and capture the actual execution plan

The work-order status report runs this query against BrennanERP. In SSMS, enable "Include Actual Execution Plan" (Ctrl+M) and run it directly against SQLDBA01:

```sql
SET STATISTICS TIME ON;

SELECT wo.WorkOrderID, wo.ScheduledStartDate, wo.Status,
       m.MachineName, m.Location
FROM dbo.WorkOrders AS wo
JOIN dbo.Machines AS m ON wo.MachineID = m.MachineID
WHERE wo.Status = 'Scheduled'
  AND wo.ScheduledStartDate >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, GETDATE());
```

The Messages tab reports roughly 52 seconds of elapsed time, and the graphical plan shows a Clustered Index Scan on WorkOrders carrying 61% of the query's total cost — SQL Server is reading every row in the table to find the small number that match the WHERE clause, because there's no index that leads with Status or ScheduledStartDate.

## Step 2 — Rule out fragmentation and stale statistics before indexing

Before concluding the only answer is a new index, confirm the existing indexes on WorkOrders aren't simply fragmented or working from stale statistics, which can make an otherwise fine index look useless:

```sql
SELECT i.name AS index_name, ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent, ips.page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID('BrennanERP'), OBJECT_ID('dbo.WorkOrders'), NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') ips
JOIN sys.indexes i ON ips.object_id = i.object_id AND ips.index_id = i.index_id;

SELECT STATS_DATE(OBJECT_ID('dbo.WorkOrders'), stats_id) AS last_updated, name
FROM sys.stats
WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('dbo.WorkOrders');
```

Fragmentation is low and statistics are current — confirming the problem really is a missing index, not routine maintenance drift that lesson 10's Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance job would already be handling.

## Step 3 — Read SQL Server's own missing-index recommendation

Rather than guess which columns to index, query the missing-index DMVs directly — they reflect exactly what the optimizer already wanted while running the plan above:

```sql
SELECT mid.statement AS table_name,
       migs.avg_user_impact,
       migs.user_seeks,
       mid.equality_columns,
       mid.inequality_columns,
       mid.included_columns
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_details AS mid
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups AS mig ON mid.index_handle = mig.index_handle
JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats AS migs ON mig.index_group_handle = migs.group_handle
WHERE mid.statement LIKE '%WorkOrders%'
ORDER BY migs.avg_user_impact DESC;
```

The result points at `Status` as the equality column, `ScheduledStartDate` as the inequality column, with `MachineID` recommended as an included column — and an estimated 93% average impact on this query's cost.

## Step 4 — Apply a real, explicitly named index

Rather than accept SQL Server's generated index name, create it with a name the team will actually recognize later:

```sql
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_WorkOrders_Status_ScheduledStartDate
ON dbo.WorkOrders (Status, ScheduledStartDate)
INCLUDE (MachineID)
WITH (ONLINE = ON);
```

`WITH (ONLINE = ON)` keeps the WorkOrders table available for the production floor's own inserts and updates while the index builds, which matters on a table that's actively written to during a shift. Because BrennanERP is protected by BrennanAG, this index build also replicates to SQLDBA02 as part of the same synchronous-commit data movement — no separate step is needed to apply it on the secondary.

## Step 5 — Re-run the query and measure the actual improvement

With "Include Actual Execution Plan" still on, run the exact same query again:

```sql
SET STATISTICS TIME ON;

SELECT wo.WorkOrderID, wo.ScheduledStartDate, wo.Status,
       m.MachineName, m.Location
FROM dbo.WorkOrders AS wo
JOIN dbo.Machines AS m ON wo.MachineID = m.MachineID
WHERE wo.Status = 'Scheduled'
  AND wo.ScheduledStartDate >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, GETDATE());
```

The plan now shows an Index Seek against `IX_WorkOrders_Status_ScheduledStartDate` instead of a Clustered Index Scan, and the Messages tab reports roughly 0.4 seconds of elapsed time — down from 52 seconds. That before/after pair, not just the new index existing, is the actual evidence this lesson set out to produce: a measured, reproducible improvement tied to one specific, intentional change.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Root-caused the work-order report slowness to a missing index — WorkOrders was being fully scanned on every run because nothing indexed Status or ScheduledStartDate. Ruled out fragmentation and stale statistics first, then pulled the recommendation straight from sys.dm_db_missing_index_details rather than guessing, built IX_WorkOrders_Status_ScheduledStartDate online so it didn't block the floor's writes, and re-ran the same query to confirm: 52 seconds down to about 0.4 seconds, with the plan now showing an index seek instead of a scan.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The slow work-order report the production supervisors flagged has been fixed and verified — what used to take almost a minute now loads in under a second. This was a measured fix, not a guess: we confirmed the actual cause first, then confirmed the actual improvement afterward with the same query run both ways.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The daily production report that was frustrating the shop floor team now loads almost instantly instead of taking nearly a minute. This was a small, targeted fix with no downtime for the floor.

lessons.title: Setting Up Azure Blob Storage as an Off-Site Backup Target
lessons.summary: Closing the real gap in lesson 10's backup automation: a copy of every BrennanERP backup now lands off-site, in Azure Blob Storage, so a fire or flood at Brennan's own building can't also take out the only copies of its backups.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding: Lesson 10 built a fully automated, test-verified backup chain for BrennanERP — but every one of those backups still lands on a local file share at Brennan's own building. A fire, a flood, or a stolen server rack would take out the database and its only backups in the same event. This lesson closes that gap by standing up an Azure Storage account, **brennansqlbackups**, with a container named **offsite-backups**, and wiring SQL Server's native backup-to-URL capability — through the same dbatools automation from lesson 10 — to write a copy of every backup there.
lessons.explainSimple: Keeping your only backup copy in the same building as the thing it's backing up is like keeping your spare house key taped under your own doormat — if anything happens to the house, the spare key is gone too. This lesson mails a second copy of the spare key to a location across town, automatically, every single time a new one gets made.
lessons.explainProfessional: Backup-to-URL lets SQL Server write a backup directly to an Azure Blob Storage container over HTTPS, authenticated with a SQL Server credential tied to a SAS token rather than a storage account key — scoped permissions, an expiration date, and no account-wide key sitting in a credential store. Folding this into the same dbatools pipeline from lesson 10, rather than standing up a second, separate off-site process, is what keeps the backup strategy coherent: one schedule, one set of jobs, one place the DBA team looks to confirm backups ran — just now with two destinations instead of one.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 — Create the storage account and container

Using Azure CLI, create the storage account and the container that will hold Brennan's off-site backups:

```bash
az storage account create \
  --name brennansqlbackups \
  --resource-group rg-brennan-infra \
  --location eastus2 \
  --sku Standard_GRS \
  --kind StorageV2

az storage container create \
  --name offsite-backups \
  --account-name brennansqlbackups \
  --auth-mode login
```

`Standard_GRS` geo-replicates the storage account itself, so Brennan's off-site backups aren't resting on a single Azure region either.

## Step 2 — Generate a SAS token scoped to just this container

Rather than hand SQL Server the storage account's master key, generate a SAS token limited to read/write/list/create on just `offsite-backups`, with an expiration date:

```bash
az storage container generate-sas \
  --name offsite-backups \
  --account-name brennansqlbackups \
  --permissions rwcl \
  --expiry 2027-10-23 \
  --https-only \
  --output tsv
```

## Step 3 — Create the SQL Server credential from that SAS token

On SQLDBA01, create a credential whose identity is literally `SHARED ACCESS SIGNATURE` — that's the required, fixed value for SAS-based backup-to-URL — and whose secret is the token generated above (without its leading `?`):

```sql
CREATE CREDENTIAL [https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups]
WITH IDENTITY = 'SHARED ACCESS SIGNATURE',
SECRET = '<sas-token-value>';
```

The credential's name must exactly match the container URL SQL Server will back up to — that's how SQL Server maps a given URL back to the right credential at backup time. Create the identical credential on SQLDBA02 as well, so either replica can write an off-site backup after a failover without an extra manual step.

## Step 4 — Run a real backup-to-URL statement

```sql
BACKUP DATABASE BrennanERP
TO URL = 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups/BrennanERP_Full_20261023.bak'
WITH CREDENTIAL = 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups',
COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM, STATS = 10;
```

## Step 5 — Fold it into the lesson-10 dbatools automation

Backup-DbaDatabase supports Azure Blob Storage as a destination directly, which means the off-site copy becomes one more parameter on the exact same job that already runs the local backup, rather than a second pipeline to maintain:

```powershell
Backup-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database BrennanERP `
    -Type Full `
    -AzureBaseUrl 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups' `
    -AzureCredential 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups' `
    -CompressBackup -Checksum
```

Added as a second step on the existing `BrennanERP - Full Backup` SQL Server Agent job from lesson 10, every nightly full backup now lands in both places automatically: the local share for fast, same-site restores, and `offsite-backups` in Azure for the scenario where the local share isn't there anymore either.

## Step 6 — Prove the off-site copy is restorable too, not just present

A backup sitting in Azure that has never been restored is exactly the same unproven risk lesson 10 solved for the local copies. Test-DbaLastBackup can restore directly from the Azure URL as well, closing the loop on the off-site copy the same way:

```powershell
Test-DbaLastBackup -SqlInstance SQLDBA02 -Database BrennanERP `
    -AzureCredential 'https://brennansqlbackups.blob.core.windows.net/offsite-backups' `
    -DataDirectory 'D:\DBATools\TestRestore\Data' `
    -LogDirectory 'D:\DBATools\TestRestore\Log' |
    Select-Object SourceServer, Database, RestoreResult, DbccResult
```

With this step added to the existing weekly verification job, BrennanERP now has two genuinely independent, test-verified backup copies: one on-site for fast restores, and one in `offsite-backups` that survives an event at Brennan's own building.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Off-site backup target is live: storage account brennansqlbackups, container offsite-backups, GRS-replicated. Authenticated with a SAS-token credential scoped to just that container, not the account key, with a hard expiration date I've put on our calendar for renewal, and the same credential created on both SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02. Added as a second step on the existing BrennanERP full-backup job from lesson 10 via Backup-DbaDatabase's AzureBaseUrl parameter, and the off-site copy now gets the same Test-DbaLastBackup restore verification the local copy already had.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've closed a real risk in our backup strategy: backups were only ever stored in the same building as the servers they protect. As of today, every nightly backup also writes a verified, encrypted copy to Microsoft Azure's cloud storage automatically, with no change to anyone's daily workflow.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our backups are no longer only stored on-site. A secure, automatic, tested copy now goes to Microsoft's cloud every night, so even in a worst-case event at our own building — fire, flood, theft — we would not lose our data.

lessons.title: Monitoring the Availability Group and Automation Jobs
lessons.summary: Building a real, scheduled health check for BrennanAG's replica and database sync state, and dbatools-based alerting on the automation jobs that keep Brennan Manufacturing's backups running -- so a problem is caught by a script, not by someone noticing days later.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
BrennanWSFC, BrennanAG, and the dbatools-based backup automation are all built and running -- but right now, the only way anyone finds out any of it has stopped working is by opening SQL Server Management Studio and looking, which in practice means nobody finds out until something worse surfaces first. This lesson builds the two checks that actually close that gap: a scheduled query against `sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states` and `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states` that reports whether `BrennanAG` is healthy and how far behind the secondary is right now, and a dbatools script that checks every SQL Agent job on `SQLDBA01` and `SQLDBA02` and raises an alert the moment one of the backup or maintenance jobs fails a run.

Neither of these is new SQL Server knowledge -- it's the same health information any DBA already knows to check by hand, now running on its own schedule, so a failed log backup or a replica that's fallen behind gets caught in minutes, not discovered during the next outage.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a lifeguard who only checks the pool when someone happens to walk by and ask if everything's okay. Most days that's fine -- but the one day it isn't fine is exactly the day nobody happened to walk by. A much better setup is a lifeguard who checks the pool on a timer, every few minutes, whether anyone asks or not.

That's what we're building for Brennan Manufacturing's database setup: instead of waiting for someone to open a screen and look, a script checks the health of the backup system (`BrennanAG`) and the nightly automation jobs on a fixed schedule, and it speaks up the moment something looks wrong -- it doesn't wait to be asked.
lessons.explainProfessional:
An Availability Group that nobody is actively monitoring is only as trustworthy as the last time someone happened to look at it, and the two numbers that matter most for AlwaysOn health are both exposed directly through DMVs rather than anything exotic: `sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states` tells you whether each replica considers itself connected and synchronization-healthy, and `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states` tells you, per database, exactly how much committed data on the primary hasn't yet made it to the secondary -- the log send queue -- and how much of what has arrived hasn't yet been replayed -- the redo queue. A growing log send queue is the earliest real warning sign of a secondary that's falling behind and quietly increasing the amount of data Brennan Manufacturing would lose in an actual failover, which is exactly the kind of degradation that's invisible unless something is actually watching for it.

The second half of this lesson closes a related but distinct gap: the dbatools-based backup automation already running on `SQLDBA01`/`SQLDBA02` executes as ordinary SQL Agent jobs, and a SQL Agent job that silently starts failing every night looks, from the outside, exactly like a SQL Agent job that's succeeding -- until someone actually needs last night's backup. `Get-DbaAgentJob` surfaces each job's last run outcome across both instances in one call, which is the one honest signal that a job genuinely ran and genuinely succeeded, as opposed to merely being scheduled.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Check replica health the way SQL Server itself tracks it

`sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states` is where SQL Server records whether each replica in `BrennanAG` considers itself connected and synchronized, joined back to `sys.availability_replicas` to get a readable server name:

```sql
SELECT ar.replica_server_name,
       rs.role_desc,
       rs.connected_state_desc,
       rs.synchronization_health_desc,
       rs.last_connect_error_description
FROM sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states rs
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON rs.replica_id = ar.replica_id
JOIN sys.availability_groups ag ON ar.group_id = ag.group_id
WHERE ag.name = 'BrennanAG';
```

On a healthy day this returns `SQLDBA01` as `PRIMARY`/`CONNECTED`/`HEALTHY` and `SQLDBA02` as `SECONDARY`/`CONNECTED`/`HEALTHY`. Anything other than `HEALTHY` or `CONNECTED` is the first sign something needs attention before it becomes an incident.

## Step 2 -- Watch the number that predicts real data-loss exposure

Replica-level health doesn't tell you how current `BrennanERP` actually is on the secondary. `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states` does, down to the specific database:

```sql
SELECT db.name AS database_name,
       ar.replica_server_name,
       drs.synchronization_state_desc,
       drs.synchronization_health_desc,
       drs.log_send_queue_size,
       drs.redo_queue_size,
       drs.last_commit_time
FROM sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states drs
JOIN sys.databases db ON drs.database_id = db.database_id
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON drs.replica_id = ar.replica_id;
```

`log_send_queue_size` growing over time means committed transactions on `SQLDBA01` are piling up faster than `SQLDBA02` can receive them -- the real-time measure of how much data Brennan Manufacturing would actually lose if `SQLDBA01` went down right now. `redo_queue_size` growing means the secondary has the data but hasn't caught up on applying it, which matters just as much for how current a failover target actually is.

## Step 3 -- Turn both checks into one scheduled job, not a manual habit

Wrap Steps 1-2 into a single stored procedure, `dbo.usp_CheckAGHealth`, that writes any non-healthy result to a log table and raises `sp_notify_operator` if anything fails the check. A SQL Agent job, `AG Health Check`, runs it every 5 minutes on `SQLDBA01`. Five minutes is deliberately tight -- this is a cheap DMV read, and a growing log send queue is far more useful caught early than caught at the next person's convenience.

## Step 4 -- Alert on automation job failures with dbatools

The nightly backup and maintenance jobs built earlier in this engagement run as ordinary SQL Agent jobs on both nodes, and a job that fails silently every night looks identical from a distance to one that's succeeding:

```powershell
$jobStatus = Get-DbaAgentJob -SqlInstance SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 |
  Where-Object { $_.Enabled -and $_.LastRunOutcome -ne 'Succeeded' }

if ($jobStatus) {
  $body = ($jobStatus | Select-Object ComputerName, Name, LastRunOutcome, LastRunDate |
    ConvertTo-Html -Fragment)
  Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $TeamsWebhookUrl -Method Post -ContentType 'application/json' `
    -Body (@{ text = "BrennanWSFC job failure:`n$body" } | ConvertTo-Json)
}
```

This runs as a Windows scheduled task every 15 minutes on `SQLDBA01`, checking both nodes in one call so a failure on either server reaches the team the same way.

## Step 5 -- Meanwhile, a completely routine request comes in

In the middle of this same week, the production-scheduling team opens a ticket asking for a new, standalone database, `ProductionSchedulingDB`, on `SQLDBA01`, to back a new scheduling module going live next month. There's nothing unusual about the request, and nothing wrong with the work: create the database normally, size it, set recovery model to `FULL` so it fits the existing backup chain, and hand it back to the application team.

```sql
CREATE DATABASE ProductionSchedulingDB
ON PRIMARY (NAME = ProductionSchedulingDB_Data, FILENAME = 'D:\SQLData\ProductionSchedulingDB.mdf', SIZE = 512MB, FILEGROWTH = 128MB)
LOG ON (NAME = ProductionSchedulingDB_Log, FILENAME = 'L:\SQLLogs\ProductionSchedulingDB.ldf', SIZE = 128MB, FILEGROWTH = 64MB);
GO
ALTER DATABASE ProductionSchedulingDB SET RECOVERY FULL;
```

As covered when `BrennanAG` was first built, creating a database and placing it under AG protection are two genuinely separate manual steps in SQL Server -- nothing makes the second one happen automatically just because the first one did. `ProductionSchedulingDB` is scheduled to be added to `BrennanAG` once the module's go-live date is firmer, and the ticket gets closed as delivered. The health-check job built in Step 3 is watching `BrennanAG` and `BrennanERP` right now -- it has no way to know this new database exists at all, which is exactly the shape of gap the rest of this engagement eventually runs into.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a 5-minute scheduled health check against sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states and sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states so a degraded replica or a growing log send/redo queue on BrennanAG gets caught immediately instead of discovered during an incident. Added a dbatools job-failure check -- Get-DbaAgentJob across SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 -- posting to Teams the moment any backup or maintenance job's last run outcome isn't Succeeded. Also delivered a routine request this week: created ProductionSchedulingDB on SQLDBA01 as a standalone database, recovery model FULL, scheduled to be added to BrennanAG once the new module's go-live date is confirmed.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The Availability Group and the nightly automation jobs are now actively monitored on a schedule instead of checked by hand when someone remembers -- any sync problem or job failure now reaches the team within minutes. Also closed a routine ticket this week: a new standalone database for the production-scheduling team's upcoming module, created and handed back; bringing it under the same AG protection is tracked as a short follow-up once that module's launch date firms up.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Our backup and failover system now watches itself and tells us immediately if anything stops working correctly, instead of us finding out the hard way. We also delivered a routine request from the scheduling team this week for their new module's database.

lessons.title: Bringing MongoDB Under Real DBA Discipline
lessons.summary: A first real pass at brennan-mongo-01's iot_sensor_logs database -- discovering it has no authentication at all, locking it down with role-based access control, and setting up real scheduled mongodump backups and basic monitoring.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Not every database at Brennan Manufacturing is SQL Server. The plant floor's sensor-collection system writes continuously into `iot_sensor_logs`, a MongoDB database on a server named `brennan-mongo-01` that has run, by all accounts, completely unmanaged since whoever stood it up moved on to other work. This lesson is the first time it gets a real DBA's attention: connecting to it for the first time to see exactly what's actually configured, finding out it has no authentication at all, locking that down with real role-based access control, and then giving it the two things every other database in this engagement already has -- scheduled, verified backups and basic ongoing monitoring.

None of this is new DBA thinking. It's the exact same discipline already applied to `BrennanERP` -- know who can touch the data, back it up on a schedule, watch that it's healthy -- applied to a platform that just happens not to be SQL Server.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine finding out that one filing cabinet in the building has never had a lock on it -- anyone who walks by can open any drawer, and nobody has ever once made a copy of what's inside in case the cabinet gets damaged. That's not really a MongoDB problem or a SQL Server problem, it's just a cabinet nobody has taken care of yet.

So the fix is exactly what you'd do with any filing cabinet: put a real lock on it, decide who actually gets a key and what each person's key opens, and start making regular copies of what's inside and storing those copies somewhere safe. The only thing different about this cabinet is which kind of lock it takes.
lessons.explainProfessional:
MongoDB installs with authentication disabled by default unless someone explicitly turns it on during setup, and an unmanaged instance that nobody has circled back to is one of the more common ways a database ends up fully exposed to anything that can reach its port, with zero audit trail of who read or wrote what. The first and most urgent finding here isn't a performance problem or a backup gap -- it's that `brennan-mongo-01` has been running this way the entire time `iot_sensor_logs` has existed, which makes access control, not backups, the first thing to fix, since a backup strategy is worth very little on a database anyone can already read or modify directly.

Once access control is real, the remaining gaps are the same ones `BrennanERP` would have had before this entire engagement started: no scheduled backup, and no one watching whether the server is actually healthy day to day. `mongodump` is MongoDB's equivalent of a native SQL Server backup -- a full logical export of a database that can be restored with `mongorestore` -- and wrapping it in a scheduled script with real retention is the direct cross-platform equivalent of the dbatools-based backup jobs already running against `BrennanERP`. The DBA judgment doesn't change between platforms; only the commands do.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Connect and see what's actually there

First real look at the server, using the `mongosh` shell:

```bash
mongosh "mongodb://brennan-mongo-01:27017"
```

It connects with no username or password prompt at all. Confirming it directly:

```javascript
db.runCommand({ connectionStatus: 1 })
// authenticatedUsers: [] -- nobody authenticated, and nothing stopped this connection
show dbs
// iot_sensor_logs   4.2GB
```

Checking the running configuration confirms why:

```bash
mongosh --eval "db.serverCmdLineOpts()" | grep -A2 security
# security: (not present in the config at all)
```

There is no `security.authorization` setting, no users collection with any real entries beyond defaults, and the server is bound to the network, not just localhost. Any machine that can reach port 27017 currently has full read and write access to every sensor reading this plant has ever collected.

## Step 2 -- Create an admin user before touching anything else

Access control has to be enabled from inside the database before it can be enforced, so the first user gets created while the door is still open:

```javascript
use admin
db.createUser({
  user: "brennan_dba_admin",
  pwd: passwordPrompt(),
  roles: [ { role: "userAdminAnyDatabase", db: "admin" }, "readWriteAnyDatabase" ]
})
```

## Step 3 -- Turn on authentication for real

Edit `mongod.conf` to require it, then restart the service:

```yaml
security:
  authorization: enabled
```

```bash
net stop MongoDB
net start MongoDB
```

From this point forward, every connection to `brennan-mongo-01` must authenticate -- confirmed by trying the Step 1 connection again and getting rejected without credentials.

## Step 4 -- Scope a real application user to exactly the one database it needs

The sensor-collection service doesn't need admin rights -- it needs to read and write `iot_sensor_logs` and nothing else:

```javascript
use iot_sensor_logs
db.createUser({
  user: "svc_sensor_ingest",
  pwd: passwordPrompt(),
  roles: [ { role: "readWrite", db: "iot_sensor_logs" } ]
})
```

The sensor service's connection string is updated to authenticate as `svc_sensor_ingest` against `iot_sensor_logs` specifically, not as the admin account -- the same least-privilege principle already applied to every SQL Server login in this engagement.

## Step 5 -- Set up real scheduled backups with mongodump

```powershell
$stamp = Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd_HHmmss
$out = "D:\MongoBackups\iot_sensor_logs_$stamp"
mongodump --host brennan-mongo-01 --db iot_sensor_logs `
  --username brennan_dba_admin --authenticationDatabase admin `
  --out $out
Get-ChildItem "D:\MongoBackups" -Directory |
  Where-Object { $_.CreationTime -lt (Get-Date).AddDays(-14) } |
  Remove-Item -Recurse -Force
```

Scheduled nightly via Windows Task Scheduler on `brennan-mongo-01`, 14-day local retention, with the same output folder also covered by the existing off-site Azure Blob Storage copy pattern already protecting the SQL Server backups.

## Step 6 -- Confirm the backup actually restores

```bash
mongorestore --host brennan-mongo-01 --username brennan_dba_admin --authenticationDatabase admin \
  --db iot_sensor_logs_restoretest "D:\MongoBackups\iot_sensor_logs_20261023_020000\iot_sensor_logs"
```

`iot_sensor_logs_restoretest` comes back with real documents, confirming the dump is genuinely restorable, and the throwaway database is dropped immediately after.

## Step 7 -- Add basic ongoing monitoring

```bash
mongostat --host brennan-mongo-01 --username brennan_dba_admin --authenticationDatabase admin --rowcount 1
```

A simple scheduled script checks `db.serverStatus().connections` and `db.stats()` on `iot_sensor_logs` daily, logging connection counts and storage size so a sudden spike -- a stuck ingestion job, a runaway client -- gets noticed the same way an AG health alert gets noticed, instead of three months from now when the disk fills up.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: First real audit of brennan-mongo-01 found authentication completely disabled -- no users, no authorization setting, bound to the network. Enabled security.authorization, created a scoped admin user plus a least-privilege svc_sensor_ingest user limited to readWrite on iot_sensor_logs only, and updated the sensor service's connection string accordingly. Added nightly mongodump backups with 14-day retention plus an off-site Azure copy, verified one restore end to end, and added daily connection/storage monitoring.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found that the plant's sensor database had zero access control since it was first stood up -- anyone on the network could read or change it. That's now locked down with real user accounts and least-privilege access, and it has scheduled, tested backups and basic monitoring for the first time, bringing it in line with how every other production database in this engagement is already managed.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found a real gap: the sensor-data system running the plant floor had no password protection at all, and no backups. That's fixed now -- proper access control, nightly backups we've verified actually work, and ongoing monitoring, the same standard of care the ERP database already has.

lessons.title: A Failover Test Reveals a Database That Never Made It Into the AG
lessons.summary: The first real failover test of BrennanAG since go-live: BrennanERP fails over cleanly, but the production-scheduling module immediately breaks -- and a methodical check of sys.databases and sys.availability_databases_cluster proves ProductionSchedulingDB was never actually part of the Availability Group.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`BrennanAG` has been running since it was built, correctly configured, synchronized, and healthy by every check in the last two lessons -- but never once actually failed over for real. This lesson is that first real test: a planned, scheduled failover of `BrennanAG` from `SQLDBA01` to `SQLDBA02`, run during a maintenance window specifically to prove the whole setup works before Brennan Manufacturing ever needs it to work during a real incident. `BrennanERP` fails over exactly as designed. Almost immediately afterward, the production-scheduling module starts throwing errors that its database simply isn't there.

The rest of this lesson is a methodical, evidence-based investigation -- not a guess, not an immediate failback -- that proves `BrennanERP` is healthy on the new primary, then proves `ProductionSchedulingDB` is sitting untouched on what's now the secondary node, still online, still fine, and was never actually a member of `BrennanAG` at all.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a two-story house with a backup generator that's supposed to power the whole house if the lights go out. Everyone's tested the switch, and it's never actually been flipped for real. One day it finally gets flipped on purpose, just to check -- and the living room lights come on perfectly. But the home office down the hall stays completely dark.

It turns out the home office was wired in after the generator was installed, and nobody ever ran its wire back to the generator -- it was still only wired to the original power line. The generator isn't broken. The living room proves that. The home office was just never actually connected to it in the first place.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The instinct after an unexpected failure during a planned test is to reverse the test immediately -- fail back, assume something is broken, make the error stop. That instinct gets set aside here in favor of verification, because failing back without understanding what actually happened just relocates an unknown problem instead of identifying it. The investigation proceeds in a specific, narrowing order: first confirm the thing that's supposed to have moved actually moved and is healthy, then check the thing that's actually broken directly, rather than through the application that's reporting the symptom.

`BrennanERP` gets checked first and clears immediately -- it's reachable through `BrennanAGListener`, its data is current, and `sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states` shows it `SYNCHRONIZED` on both nodes. That single result already rules out a broken failover mechanism; `BrennanAG` itself did exactly what it was built to do. `ProductionSchedulingDB` is checked next, and not through the application -- directly, with `sys.databases` on `SQLDBA01`, the node that just became secondary. It's `ONLINE`. It's untouched. And a direct query against `sys.availability_databases_cluster`, which lists only the databases SQL Server itself considers part of a given Availability Group, confirms the actual finding: `ProductionSchedulingDB` was never a member of `BrennanAG` at any point. This isn't a failover bug. It's a database that was simply never inside the thing that just failed over.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Run the failover test that should have happened before now

With `BrennanAG` built, synchronized, and monitored, but never actually tested end to end, a planned manual failover gets scheduled during a Thursday-night maintenance window:

```sql
-- Connected to SQLDBA02 (the current secondary, about to become primary)
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG FAILOVER;
```

This is a planned, synchronous failover against a healthy, synchronized secondary -- it should complete in seconds, with zero data loss, promoting `SQLDBA02` to primary and demoting `SQLDBA01` to secondary.

## Step 2 -- Two different outcomes, immediately

Within a minute, `BrennanERP` is reachable and current through `BrennanAGListener` -- the application team confirms orders and inventory lookups are working normally. At the same time, the production-scheduling module -- the one built on `ProductionSchedulingDB`, created a few weeks earlier -- starts throwing connection errors:

```
[ERROR] Cannot open database "ProductionSchedulingDB" requested by the login.
The database could not be found or the current user does not have
permission to access it.
```

The temptation is to assume the failover itself is broken and fail back immediately. That gets set aside in favor of checking exactly what did and didn't move correctly.

## Step 3 -- Confirm BrennanERP failed over cleanly first

Querying directly against the new primary, `SQLDBA02`:

```sql
SELECT db.name, drs.synchronization_state_desc, drs.synchronization_health_desc,
       drs.log_send_queue_size, drs.redo_queue_size
FROM sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states drs
JOIN sys.databases db ON drs.database_id = db.database_id
WHERE db.name = 'BrennanERP';
```

`BrennanERP` reports `SYNCHRONIZED` / `HEALTHY`, with both queue sizes at zero. A quick row-count check against a known table confirms current data on the new primary. This rules out a broken or partial failover -- `BrennanAG` itself did exactly what it was supposed to do.

## Step 4 -- Check ProductionSchedulingDB directly, not through the application

Connecting to `SQLDBA01` -- the node that just became the secondary:

```sql
SELECT name, state_desc, recovery_model_desc, create_date
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = 'ProductionSchedulingDB';
```

```
name                     state_desc   recovery_model_desc   create_date
ProductionSchedulingDB   ONLINE       FULL                   2026-10-xx
```

`ProductionSchedulingDB` is sitting there, completely fine, `ONLINE`, exactly where it was created. It was never touched by the failover at all -- which, for a database that's genuinely part of an Availability Group, would be impossible; AG member databases change role along with the replica itself.

## Step 5 -- Prove it was never actually in BrennanAG

`sys.availability_databases_cluster` lists only the databases SQL Server's cluster metadata considers part of a given Availability Group -- the authoritative answer, not an inference:

```sql
SELECT adc.database_name, ag.name AS availability_group_name
FROM sys.availability_databases_cluster adc
JOIN sys.availability_groups ag ON adc.group_id = ag.group_id
WHERE ag.name = 'BrennanAG';
```

The result lists `BrennanERP`. It does not list `ProductionSchedulingDB` at all. That settles it: the production-scheduling module isn't broken because the failover went wrong -- it's broken because the database behind it was never a member of `BrennanAG` in the first place, so when `SQLDBA01` stopped being the primary, there was nothing protecting `ProductionSchedulingDB` from becoming unreachable to anything still pointed at the old primary role.

## Step 6 -- Leave it right where it is for the next step

Nothing gets changed yet. `ProductionSchedulingDB` stays exactly as found on `SQLDBA01`, and `BrennanAG` stays failed over to `SQLDBA02` -- the next lesson needs both of those facts undisturbed to trace exactly when this gap was created and fix it properly, rather than papering over it with an immediate failback.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran the first real failover drill against BrennanAG. BrennanERP failed over cleanly -- confirmed SYNCHRONIZED/HEALTHY on SQLDBA02 with zero queue lag -- so the AG mechanism itself is proven sound. ProductionSchedulingDB broke immediately after; sys.databases on SQLDBA01 shows it ONLINE and untouched, and sys.availability_databases_cluster confirms it was never a member of BrennanAG at all. Root cause is scope, not a failover defect.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Our first real test of the failover system found a real gap, and we've already confirmed it is not a problem with the failover system itself -- the core ERP database moved over perfectly. A second, newer database was never actually brought under that same protection, and we're tracking down exactly how that happened next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We ran a planned test of our disaster-recovery setup specifically to find problems before a real outage could, and it worked -- it found one. Our core ERP system performed exactly as designed. A newer database tied to the new scheduling module was not yet protected the same way, and we're fixing that now.

lessons.title: Finding and Fixing the Missing Database and the Process Gap Behind It
lessons.summary: Confirming when ProductionSchedulingDB was created, adding it to BrennanAG for real with a backup/restore-with-norecovery sequence, re-running the failover test to prove it, and closing the real process gap with a recurring automated check for any unprotected database.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved exactly what's wrong: `ProductionSchedulingDB` was created correctly as a standalone database and simply never added to `BrennanAG`. This lesson fixes it properly -- failing `BrennanAG` back to `SQLDBA01` so the database being added is actually on the current primary, backing it up, restoring it `WITH NORECOVERY` on `SQLDBA02`, and running `ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG ADD DATABASE` -- then re-running the exact same failover test from Lesson 15 to prove, this time, that it actually works.

The lesson closes by naming the real root cause honestly: this was never a mistake anyone made carelessly. Creating a database and placing it under AG protection are two separate manual steps, and in a normal week of routine DBA work, the second step is exactly the kind of thing that gets missed. The real fix isn't just adding one database -- it's a recurring, automated check that compares every database on `SQLDBA01` against AG membership and alerts the moment any database exists without that protection, so this specific gap can't happen silently again.
lessons.explainSimple: Going back to the house with the generator: once you find out the home office was never wired to the generator, the fix has two parts. First, you actually run the wire -- connect that one room properly, and test the generator switch again to make sure the office lights come on this time too. But the smarter second part is realizing any new room added to the house in the future could have the exact same problem, so you set up a simple checklist that gets checked every time a new room gets wired, specifically asking "is this one connected to the generator too?" -- so you never find out about a gap like this during an actual power outage again.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The mechanical fix here is the standard, well-established process for adding an existing database to an Availability Group after the fact: a full backup on the current primary, a restore `WITH NORECOVERY` on the secondary so it's left in a state the AG join can take over, and then the `ADD DATABASE` command itself, which only works against a database that's already in that exact restoring state on every secondary replica. None of that is new -- it's the same mechanism that put `BrennanERP` into `BrennanAG` in the first place, just run again, later, for a second database.

The root-cause finding is what actually matters for preventing a repeat. The gap wasn't negligence -- `ProductionSchedulingDB` was created correctly, sized correctly, and set to the right recovery model. The gap was that SQL Server has no mechanism that automatically protects a new database just because it happens to live on a server that also hosts an AG, and nothing in the existing Lesson 13 health check was watching for databases that exist but aren't AG members, because that check was only ever designed to watch databases already known to be in scope. The fix that actually closes this permanently is a recurring comparison between `sys.databases` and `sys.availability_databases_cluster` -- the same two views used to diagnose the problem in Lesson 15, now running on a schedule instead of only during an investigation.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm when the gap was actually created

```sql
SELECT name, create_date
FROM sys.databases
WHERE name = 'ProductionSchedulingDB';
```

The `create_date` lines up with the routine new-database request handled during this week's monitoring work -- confirming this was a real, ordinary ticket that simply never had its second step followed up, not a database that appeared through some unrelated mistake.

## Step 2 -- Fail BrennanAG back to SQLDBA01 before adding the database

`ProductionSchedulingDB` only exists on `SQLDBA01`, so it needs to be added while `SQLDBA01` is the primary:

```sql
-- Connected to SQLDBA01
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG FAILOVER;
```

Confirming the role swapped back cleanly before continuing, the same way Lesson 15 confirmed it the first time:

```sql
SELECT ar.replica_server_name, rs.role_desc
FROM sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states rs
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON rs.replica_id = ar.replica_id;
-- SQLDBA01 -> PRIMARY, SQLDBA02 -> SECONDARY
```

## Step 3 -- Back it up on the primary, restore WITH NORECOVERY on the secondary

```sql
-- On SQLDBA01 (primary)
BACKUP DATABASE ProductionSchedulingDB
TO DISK = 'D:\SQLBackups\ProductionSchedulingDB_Full.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM;

BACKUP LOG ProductionSchedulingDB
TO DISK = 'D:\SQLBackups\ProductionSchedulingDB_Log.trn' WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM;
```

```sql
-- On SQLDBA02 (secondary), after copying both backup files over
RESTORE DATABASE ProductionSchedulingDB
FROM DISK = 'D:\SQLBackups\ProductionSchedulingDB_Full.bak' WITH NORECOVERY;

RESTORE LOG ProductionSchedulingDB
FROM DISK = 'D:\SQLBackups\ProductionSchedulingDB_Log.trn' WITH NORECOVERY;
```

`WITH NORECOVERY` leaves the database on `SQLDBA02` in exactly the restoring state the AG join requires -- a database that's already been recovered normally cannot be added to an AG.

## Step 4 -- Add it to the Availability Group for real

```sql
-- On SQLDBA01 (primary)
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG ADD DATABASE ProductionSchedulingDB;
```

Confirming it joined and is actively synchronizing:

```sql
SELECT db.name, drs.synchronization_state_desc, drs.synchronization_health_desc
FROM sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states drs
JOIN sys.databases db ON drs.database_id = db.database_id
WHERE db.name = 'ProductionSchedulingDB';
-- SYNCHRONIZED / HEALTHY on both nodes
```

## Step 5 -- Re-run the exact same failover test and prove it this time

```sql
-- Connected to SQLDBA02
ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG FAILOVER;
```

This time, querying `ProductionSchedulingDB` through `BrennanAGListener` after the failover returns real rows immediately, and the production-scheduling team confirms the module works without a single configuration change on their end. The fix is proven, not assumed.

## Step 6 -- Close the actual root cause: build a recurring check for unprotected databases

Adding one database back doesn't stop the next one from slipping through the same way. A dbatools-based scheduled script compares every real database against AG membership, nightly:

```powershell
$allDbs = Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 |
  Where-Object { $_.Name -notin @('master','model','msdb','tempdb') }

$agDbs = Get-DbaAgDatabase -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -AvailabilityGroup BrennanAG

$unprotected = $allDbs | Where-Object { $_.Name -notin $agDbs.DatabaseName }

if ($unprotected) {
  $body = ($unprotected | Select-Object Name, CreateDate | ConvertTo-Html -Fragment)
  Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $TeamsWebhookUrl -Method Post -ContentType 'application/json' `
    -Body (@{ text = "Database(s) on SQLDBA01 not protected by BrennanAG:`n$body" } | ConvertTo-Json)
}
```

Scheduled nightly on `SQLDBA01`, feeding the same Teams channel the Lesson 13 job-failure alert already uses. Any future `ProductionSchedulingDB`-style ticket -- a database created correctly but not yet AG-joined -- now surfaces within 24 hours, as a routine alert, instead of during the next failover test.

## Step 7 -- Write the honest root cause down

```
ROOT CAUSE: Not negligence. Creating a database and joining it to BrennanAG
are two separate manual SQL Server actions; the second step on
ProductionSchedulingDB was never completed after a routine database request.
No existing monitoring was watching for databases outside the AG, because
the Lesson 13 health check was scoped only to databases already known to be
AG members.

FIX: ProductionSchedulingDB added to BrennanAG and the fix proven with a
second failover test. A nightly automated comparison of sys.databases
against sys.availability_databases_cluster now closes this exact class of
gap going forward.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Confirmed ProductionSchedulingDB's create_date matched the routine request handled during Lesson 13. Failed BrennanAG back to SQLDBA01, backed it up, restored WITH NORECOVERY on SQLDBA02, and ran ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG ADD DATABASE. Re-ran the Lesson 15 failover test and confirmed ProductionSchedulingDB now follows the AG correctly with zero application-side changes. Closed the real root cause with a nightly dbatools script comparing Get-DbaDatabase against Get-DbaAgDatabase on SQLDBA01, alerting on any database outside BrennanAG.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Found the exact cause of Thursday's failover gap: a database created correctly for the scheduling team's new module simply never had the separate step of joining it to the Availability Group completed. It's fixed and proven with a second test. More importantly, we've added an automated nightly check that catches this specific situation for any future database, so it can't recur unnoticed.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We found and fixed the real cause of the gap our test uncovered -- a new database for the scheduling module that hadn't yet been added to our backup-and-failover protection, a routine step that got missed during a normal week of work. It's fixed and verified with a second test, and we've now automated a daily check that catches this exact situation going forward, so we find it ourselves instead of during a real outage.

lessons.title: Connecting a Monitoring Dashboard for the DBA Team
lessons.summary: Wiring BrennanAG's replica health, the dbatools backup and maintenance job history, and the new AG-membership gap check into one Power BI report the whole DBA team can open any time, not just whoever happens to be at a keyboard.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Everything built across this engagement so far -- BrennanWSFC, BrennanAG, the dbatools-driven backup and maintenance automation, the WorkOrders performance fix, the off-site copy in brennansqlbackups, and the MongoDB oversight work on brennan-mongo-01 -- lives inside tools only a DBA opens: SSMS, PowerShell, Failover Cluster Manager. This video closes that gap by building a Power BI report, BrennanAG -- DBA Health, that pulls directly from data this project is already generating: replica synchronization state from sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, SQL Server Agent job outcomes for every backup, verification, and maintenance job on SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02, and -- most important after the last two lessons -- the recurring job that compares sys.databases against BrennanAG's own membership list, so a database quietly left out of the Availability Group shows up on a screen before the next failover test finds it instead.

Nothing new gets instrumented here. Every one of these signals already exists somewhere in the environment; the work is choosing which ones matter for day-to-day visibility and putting them in front of the DBA team -- and anyone else who needs a quick read on system health -- without anyone needing to open SSMS first.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a workshop with several machines running at once -- a saw, a lathe, an air compressor -- each with its own small gauge bolted onto its own housing. A good shop foreman doesn't walk to each machine every hour to read its gauge separately; eventually someone wires all those gauges into a single board on the wall, so one glance across the room tells the foreman which machine needs attention right now, before it needs attention urgently.

Brennan Manufacturing's database environment has had its own gauges the whole time: whether the two servers are in sync, whether last night's backup job actually ran, whether every database that is supposed to be protected actually is. This video wires those gauges into one board -- a single report anyone on the DBA team can open, instead of walking over to five different tools to check five different things.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Every signal this report surfaces already exists natively in the platform -- sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states for AG synchronization health, msdb job history for Agent job outcomes, and the AGMembershipCheck table the lesson 16 recurring job already writes to. The work here is deliberately curation and presentation, not instrumentation: deciding which of the available signals actually answer 'is BrennanERP's protection working right now,' and putting them in front of people who do not live in SSMS all day.

Power BI is the right tool for this specifically because it is a platform Brennan's team can already publish and share reports on without standing up a new server to patch and secure, and it is a tool non-DBA stakeholders already know how to open. The report connects in Import mode against a small DbaOps database on SQLDBA01, reached through BrennanAGListener so the report itself survives a failover without anyone touching a connection string, refreshed every 15 minutes -- frequent enough to catch a stuck replica or a failed job the same shift it happens, without hammering the listener with constant live queries. Three signals matter most: replica synchronization health (is BrennanAG actually ready to fail over right now, not just configured to be), job success and failure across every scheduled dbatools job on both nodes, and the AG-membership gap check -- the direct, permanent, visual descendant of the incident the last two lessons walked through.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Inventory what is already being logged

Before building anything new, confirm what this engagement is already writing down. The lesson 10 and lesson 16 automation already populate a small DbaOps database on SQLDBA01:

```
DbaOps.dbo.BackupVerificationLog   -- from Test-DbaLastBackup, weekly
DbaOps.dbo.MaintenanceLog          -- from Invoke-DbaDbMaintenance -LogToTable
DbaOps.dbo.AGMembershipCheck       -- from the lesson 16 recurring gap check
```

None of this is new data. It is data this project has been producing for several lessons that nobody has put in front of the team yet.

## Step 2 -- Confirm the AG-membership check is actually queryable

```sql
SELECT TOP 20 check_run_at, database_name, in_ag
FROM DbaOps.dbo.AGMembershipCheck
ORDER BY check_run_at DESC;
```

A healthy history shows every production database reporting in_ag = 1 on every run. ProductionSchedulingDB's own row history, before and after lesson 16's fix, is the literal proof this check works -- and it is the first thing worth pinning to the new report.

## Step 3 -- Wrap replica health in a view Power BI can read cleanly

DMVs cannot be queried directly by every reporting tool, so wrap the health check in a plain view inside DbaOps:

```sql
CREATE VIEW DbaOps.dbo.vw_AGReplicaHealth AS
SELECT ar.replica_server_name, drs.database_name,
       drs.synchronization_state_desc, drs.synchronization_health_desc
FROM sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states drs
JOIN sys.availability_replicas ar ON drs.replica_id = ar.replica_id;
```

## Step 4 -- Land Agent job history where the report can see it

Agent job history on SQLDBA01 and SQLDBA02 feeds a small snapshot table every 15 minutes via a dbatools-backed Agent job step:

```powershell
Get-DbaAgentJobHistory -SqlInstance SQLDBA01, SQLDBA02 -Since (Get-Date).AddHours(-24) |
    Select-Object SqlInstance, Job, RunDate, Status, Message |
    Write-DbaDbTableData -SqlInstance SQLDBA01 -Database DbaOps -Table JobHistorySnapshot -AutoCreateTable
```

## Step 5 -- Build the Power BI data model

Connect Power BI Desktop to BrennanAGListener,1433 using Import mode, and load vw_AGReplicaHealth, AGMembershipCheck, and JobHistorySnapshot. Import mode (not DirectQuery) keeps the report fast and keeps load off the listener between the 15-minute scheduled refreshes.

## Step 6 -- Build three report pages, with conditional formatting that actually means something

```
Page 1 -- AG Replica Health
  Card: synchronization_health_desc per replica. Green = HEALTHY,
  red = anything else, sustained longer than one refresh cycle.

Page 2 -- Backup & Maintenance Jobs (SQLDBA01 / SQLDBA02)
  Matrix: job name x last 7 runs, colored by Status. A single red
  cell is worth a glance; two in a row for the same job is worth a page.

Page 3 -- AG Membership Gap Check
  Table: every production database, its current in_ag flag, and the
  timestamp of its last clean check. Anything reporting in_ag = 0 is
  the direct, visual version of the exact incident lessons 15 and 16
  walked through -- caught here, now, instead of during the next drill.
```

## Step 7 -- Publish, share, and walk the team through reading it

Publish to a shared Power BI workspace, grant the DBA team and Dana's leadership chain view access, and spend ten minutes walking one person through each page live: what healthy looks like, what a single amber reading means versus a sustained one, and who gets a message if a database ever shows in_ag = 0. A dashboard nobody was shown how to read gets ignored the same way an unexplained report does.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a Power BI report, BrennanAG -- DBA Health, reading from a new DbaOps database on SQLDBA01: a vw_AGReplicaHealth view over sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states, the lesson 16 AGMembershipCheck table, and a 15-minute Agent job history snapshot. Connects through BrennanAGListener in Import mode so the report itself survives a failover. Three pages: replica health, job success/failure across both nodes, and the AG-membership gap check, which is now visible on a screen instead of only inside a scheduled job's output.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The DBA team -- and leadership -- can now check system health themselves without asking someone to pull a report. Backup job success, whether the two servers are properly in sync, and whether every database is actually protected are all visible on one live dashboard, refreshed every 15 minutes, instead of living inside tools only a DBA opens.
workplaceExplanation.executive: You can now open a report yourself and see, at a glance, whether our production database protection is actually working -- not take someone's word for it. The same gap that caused a hiccup in our last test now has its own permanent gauge on this dashboard, so it gets caught on a screen going forward, not during the next drill.

lessons.title: Presenting the Tested HA Plan and Multi-Platform Coverage to Leadership
lessons.summary: The real presentation moment -- walking Dana, Marcus, and Greg through the finished cluster, performance, automation, and MongoDB oversight work, including an honest account of the ProductionSchedulingDB gap the lesson 15 failover drill caught.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the moment the engagement has been building toward: a room with Dana Kowalski, Marcus Webb, and Greg Hollis, looking at what actually got built -- BrennanWSFC and BrennanAG protecting BrennanERP with a proven automatic failover, the WorkOrders report fix, the dbatools backup and maintenance automation, the off-site copy in brennansqlbackups, the monitoring and job-health checks from lesson 13, the dashboard from the last lesson, and brennan-mongo-01 now under real DBA discipline instead of running unmanaged. It also means walking into that room and talking, without flinching, about the gap the lesson 15 failover drill found: ProductionSchedulingDB, created correctly on SQLDBA01 for the scheduling-module expansion mentioned back in lesson 3, with the AG-join step deliberately scheduled for later -- and then never actually done before the drill ran.

The skill in this video is not technical. It is explaining a real incident honestly: what happened, why a reasonable setup still missed it, and the genuinely good news underneath the bad news -- this was caught during the first real planned failover drill BrennanAG had ever run, with zero live scheduling-module orders actually at risk, instead of during a real SQLDBA01 hardware failure. That is exactly what a tested failover plan is supposed to do.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine the plant installs a second backup generator for the whole building, and everyone agrees to actually test the switchover on a schedule instead of just trusting it works. During the first real test, the main machines switch over to backup power cleanly, exactly as planned. But one newer machine on the line goes dark anyway -- not because the generator failed, but because that machine had been wired up correctly on its own circuit, with a plan to connect it to the shared backup system later, and that second step simply never got done before the test ran. The machine itself was fine the whole time, sitting right there, untouched -- it just was not actually on the system that switches over.

That is almost exactly what happened here. A newer database had been built correctly and was running fine the whole time, but the step that would have let it switch over with everything else was scheduled for later and never actually finished. The drill is what caught it -- on a Tuesday, during a planned test, with nothing real actually at stake.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The structure of this meeting matters as much as its content: lead with what is genuinely built and working, name the ProductionSchedulingDB gap specifically rather than softening it into a vague mention of a hiccup, and close by reframing a failed drill assumption as the drill doing exactly its job. The honest version of the incident is specific, not abstract: ProductionSchedulingDB was created correctly, with its AG-join step explicitly logged as a separate task scheduled for later -- and that second step simply never got completed before the lesson 15 drill ran. During that drill, BrennanAG failed over cleanly: BrennanERP followed BrennanAGListener to SQLDBA02 without incident, exactly as designed. The scheduling module's connection to ProductionSchedulingDB broke completely, because the database was never a member of BrennanAG and therefore never existed on SQLDBA02 at all -- even though the data itself sat completely safe and untouched on SQLDBA01, now running in the secondary role.

The gap is also worth naming as more serious than the failed connection alone made it look, because being honest about severity is part of being honest at all: a database with zero redundancy anywhere is one hardware failure away from being gone entirely, and this was a planned, graceful role swap, not the kind of real failure that would have actually taken SQLDBA01 down. That is the detail that makes the good news land correctly in this meeting: the gap was found during a controlled Tuesday-morning drill, with the scheduling module's real production use still ramping up, rather than during an actual SQLDBA01 hardware failure with no copy of that data to recover from anywhere.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Open with the finished architecture, plainly, before the incident

Remind the room briefly where this started: a 48-hour production-scheduling outage on a single nine-year-old server, 12 missed ship dates, and one line losing roughly 6 hours to avoidable changeovers. That is the baseline everything below gets measured against.

```
WHAT IS BUILT AND RUNNING TODAY:

  HA:          BrennanWSFC (SQLDBA01/SQLDBA02) carrying BrennanAG,
               synchronous-commit, automatic failover, reachable
               through BrennanAGListener -- proven with a real drill
  Performance: WorkOrders report fixed and measured: ~52s down to
               ~0.4s; Query Store baseline captured and retained
  Automation:  dbatools-driven backup, restore-verification, and
               maintenance jobs on both nodes, fully scheduled
  Off-site:    Every backup also lands in brennansqlbackups (Azure
               Storage), independent of the building
  Monitoring:  The Power BI dashboard from last lesson -- replica
               health, job outcomes, and the AG-membership gap check
  Multi-platform: brennan-mongo-01 / iot_sensor_logs now has real
               backups, monitoring, and a completed access review
```

Say this part plainly -- it is real, it is in production, and it is most of the engagement.

## Step 2 -- Name the incident directly, with the specific mechanism

```
YOU: During our first real planned failover drill, BrennanAG
     switched over to SQLDBA02 exactly as designed -- BrennanERP
     followed the listener without incident. But the scheduling
     module's connection broke completely. ProductionSchedulingDB,
     created correctly for that expansion, had its AG-join step
     scheduled for later as a separate task -- and that second step
     never actually got finished before the drill ran.
```

## Step 3 -- Explain why this was a real, easy-to-miss gap

```
YOU: Creating a database and joining it to BrennanAG are two
     separate manual steps, and the second one is easy to lose track
     of once the first one is done and the database is already
     working fine for everyone using it. ProductionSchedulingDB ran
     correctly every day. Nothing about normal use ever showed this
     gap, because it only exists at the exact moment a failover
     happens, and that had never happened to this database before.
     The data itself was never at risk during the drill -- it sat
     completely safe on SQLDBA01 the whole time. What the drill
     proved is that if SQLDBA01 had suffered a real hardware failure
     instead of a planned, graceful switch, that database would have
     had no copy anywhere to recover from at all.
```

## Step 4 -- State the good news plainly, and mean it

```
YOU: This matters less than it sounds like it should, because we
     found it in a drill we ran on purpose, on a Tuesday, with no
     real production orders riding on this database yet. Nobody's
     schedule was disrupted and nothing was lost. This is exactly
     what a drill that actually unplugs a server is supposed to find.
```

## Step 5 -- Show what is in place now as a direct result

```
FIX:      ProductionSchedulingDB backed up, seeded to SQLDBA02, and
          added to BrennanAG with ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ADD DATABASE
VERIFIED: A second drill confirmed it now fails over with BrennanERP
GOING FORWARD: A recurring job compares sys.databases against
          BrennanAG membership and reports any gap on the lesson 17
          dashboard, and a formal new-database checklist (next lesson)

```

## Step 6 -- Rehearse the hard question

```
Q: How do we know there is not another one of these somewhere?
A: We do not know that with certainty -- nobody legitimately can.
   What changed is that we now have a recurring automated check whose
   entire purpose is finding exactly this gap, plus a checklist that
   stops it from happening again on a new database, instead of hoping
   none exists.
```

## Step 7 -- Close by asking for explicit sign-off

Ask Dana directly to confirm the cluster, automation, and multi-platform work are considered production-ready, and that the recurring membership check and the upcoming new-database checklist are understood as permanent, standing practice -- not a one-time fix now considered closed.
