lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
A cluster that only the person who built it can operate is not actually finished -- it is a dependency on one person, which is close to the exact risk this engagement exists to remove. This video writes the three documents that let any on-call DBA, not just you, run this environment: a step-by-step AG failover runbook; a new-database checklist that exists specifically because of the ProductionSchedulingDB incident, with adding a database to BrennanAG as its own named, unskippable line; and a platform inventory covering both SQL Server and MongoDB -- what is backed up, what is monitored, and who owns each piece.

The checklist is the direct, permanent artifact of the last two lessons. It exists so that the exact gap that caused ProductionSchedulingDB to go fully unavailable during a drill -- a database created on a protected server and quietly never protected itself -- gets checked for, by name, every single time a new database goes into production, instead of depending on anyone remembering that it happened once.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you are the only person in the shop who knows exactly how to switch production over to the backup generator -- which switch, in what order, how long it takes. That is useful right up until the day you are out sick and the power actually goes out. A real handoff means writing those steps down clearly enough that anyone on the team could follow them correctly without you there to explain.

This video writes down exactly that for Brennan's database environment: the steps to follow if the main server has a real problem, a checklist for anyone setting up a brand-new database so it never again gets skipped from the backup system by accident, and a plain list of what is backed up and watched and by whom -- clear enough that someone who was not in any of the last eighteen videos could still run this correctly.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A failover plan and a membership gap check that exist only as one DBA's working knowledge are, functionally, a single point of failure shaped exactly like the hardware failure this whole engagement was built to remove. The three documents here serve distinct audiences: the failover runbook is written for whoever is on call during a real incident and needs to execute correct steps in order without reasoning from first principles; the new-database checklist is written for whoever provisions the next database on SQLDBA01 or SQLDBA02, including a developer or product owner who has never heard of BrennanAG; and the platform inventory is written for anyone -- technical or not -- who needs to know, at a glance, what is actually protected and who is responsible for it.

The checklist's AG-membership line is the single most load-bearing item in this handoff. It exists because ProductionSchedulingDB's gap was real, silent under normal use, and genuinely dangerous -- a database with zero redundancy that nobody noticed was unprotected until a drill proved it. The only reliable defense against this recurring, on this database or the next one, is a checklist line that gets actively verified every time a new database is created on a protected server, backed by the lesson 16 automated check as a second, independent safety net rather than the only one. Writing seed-to-SQLDBA02-then-ALTER-AVAILABILITY-GROUP-ADD-DATABASE as its own numbered step is what turns one incident into a permanent process improvement instead of a story people eventually stop telling.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the AG failover runbook as a numbered, executable sequence

This engagement started because Brennan's recovery depended entirely on Greg's memory and a restore process that had never been rehearsed. The runbook below exists so recovery never again depends on one person.

```
BRENNANAG -- FAILOVER RUNBOOK

WHEN TO USE: SQLDBA01 is confirmed down or unreachable, not a
transient network blip -- check connectivity and Windows Event Log
on SQLDBA01 first if it is reachable at all.

PRE-FAILOVER CHECKLIST:
  [ ] Confirm this is a genuine node failure, not a brief hiccup
  [ ] Confirm SQLDBA02 reports SYNCHRONIZED / HEALTHY for BrennanERP
      (query sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states or check the
      lesson 17 dashboard)
  [ ] *** Confirm, via DbaOps.dbo.AGMembershipCheck, that every
      database expected to be protected actually shows in_ag = 1.
      This is the exact gap that left ProductionSchedulingDB
      unavailable during the lesson 15 drill. ***
  [ ] Notify the on-call lead and open an incident ticket

FAILOVER STEPS (automatic failover should already have triggered;
if it has not):
  1. On SQLDBA02:
       ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG FAILOVER;
  2. Confirm BrennanAGListener now resolves to SQLDBA02 and that
     applications reconnect within a few seconds with no changes
  3. Monitor the lesson 17 dashboard for job and replica health on
     the new primary for the next 30 minutes
  4. Update the incident ticket with the failover timestamp

POST-FAILOVER:
  [ ] Once SQLDBA01 is confirmed healthy, do not fail back
      immediately -- schedule failback for a low-activity window
  [ ] Log the drill or incident, including whether every database
      that should have failed over actually did
```

## Step 2 -- Write the new-database checklist -- the real artifact of this incident

```
NEW DATABASE ON A PROTECTED SERVER -- CHECKLIST
  [ ] Confirm recovery model is FULL
  [ ] Take an initial full backup
  [ ] *** Add the database to BrennanAG: back up, restore WITH
      NORECOVERY to SQLDBA02, then
        ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP BrennanAG ADD DATABASE <name>; ***
  [ ] Confirm synchronization_health_desc = HEALTHY for the new
      database specifically, not just for BrennanAG overall
  [ ] Confirm the next AGMembershipCheck run reports in_ag = 1 --
      do not wait a week to find out
  [ ] Add it to the lesson 10 dbatools backup/maintenance schedule
  [ ] Add it by name to the lesson 17 Power BI report
  [ ] A second person (DBA lead or on-call) signs off that every box
      above is checked before the database is called production-ready
```

## Step 3 -- Write the platform inventory

```
SQL SERVER
  BrennanERP      -- in BrennanAG, synchronous, auto-failover proven
  ProductionSchedulingDB -- in BrennanAG (fixed in lesson 16)
  Backups: nightly full + 15-min log, local + brennansqlbackups off-site
  Monitored: lesson 17 Power BI dashboard; owner: on-call DBA rotation

MONGODB
  brennan-mongo-01 / iot_sensor_logs
  Backups: configured and verified (lesson 13/14 work)
  Access: reviewed, least-privilege applied
  Monitored: included on its own page of the lesson 17 dashboard
  Owner: DBA team, with the product team retaining day-to-day use
```

## Step 4 -- Walk one other person through all three documents live

Spend thirty minutes walking the on-call DBA through the runbook and the checklist, including the AG-membership items specifically, and have them repeat back why each one exists.

## Step 5 -- Store all three where the next on-call DBA will actually find them

Commit the runbook, checklist, and inventory to the team's shared ops wiki, and link the checklist from the Agent job that provisions new databases so nobody has to remember where it lives.

That is what makes this durable beyond any one person.

lessons.title: Wrap-Up: What Changed, and What's Still Manual
lessons.summary: The honest closing assessment of the Brennan Manufacturing build -- what's genuinely solved, and what still depends on a human remembering to do it or hasn't actually been tested yet, including a true site-level disaster drill that's never been run.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
This is the last video in the series, and like the engagement it closes out, it is not a highlight reel. Over nineteen lessons, Brennan Manufacturing's production-scheduling database went from a single nine-year-old server with no secondary copy anywhere to a genuinely clustered, performance-tuned, automated, off-site-backed-up, and monitored environment -- with a second platform, MongoDB, brought under real DBA discipline along the way, and a real incident found and fixed in the process. That part is real, it is in production, and it is genuinely done.

What this video does instead of celebrating is the harder, more useful thing: naming exactly what is still manual, still newer and less proven, or still untested, so whoever maintains this environment next -- possibly you, months from now -- is not caught off guard by a limitation that was always there but never said out loud.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you spent months upgrading an old workshop -- new wiring, a backup generator, smoke detectors in every room. It is genuinely much safer than before. But a good contractor does not just hand over the keys and say it is perfect and walk away -- they say the smoke detector batteries still need checking twice a year, the backup generator is only as good as the last time someone actually tested it under load, and the new fire door out back has never actually been used in a real evacuation, only talked through on paper. That honesty is what keeps the workshop actually safe, instead of someone discovering a gap the hard way later.

That is this whole video: being plain about what is genuinely solid in what was built for Brennan Manufacturing, and what still needs a person checking in on it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A credible project retrospective does two things most wrap-ups skip: it states the real architecture plainly enough that someone who missed the first nineteen videos could still understand what is running, and it names the actual gaps with the same specificity the earlier lessons used for the ProductionSchedulingDB incident -- not there is room for improvement, but named, concrete limitations with a reason. For Brennan, three are worth stating without softening.

First, the new-database checklist from the last lesson is a document and a second person's sign-off, not an automated gate -- nothing in SQL Server itself stops a database from being created on SQLDBA01 without anyone running through it, and the lesson 16 recurring check only catches a skipped step after the fact, on its next scheduled run, not before a database goes live. Second, MongoDB's discipline is real but genuinely newer: brennan-mongo-01 now has verified backups, monitoring, and a completed access review, but it has no replica set and no automatic failover the way BrennanAG gives BrennanERP -- a hardware failure on that one Mongo server today would mean a real restore, not a seconds-long failover, and that gap is honest, not hidden. Third, every failover this project has proven -- including the one that caught ProductionSchedulingDB -- has been an in-cluster test, taking one node down while the rest of the building, the network, and SQLDBA02's own site stayed fully available. A true site-level disaster, the whole building affected at once, would depend on the off-site backup copy in brennansqlbackups and the slower, hours-scale recovery time written down back in lesson 2 -- and that specific scenario has never actually been rehearsed end to end. Naming these is not an admission of failure; overselling completeness to a stakeholder is itself the kind of trust problem the ProductionSchedulingDB incident already taught this room to take seriously. The honest version of done is this solved the specific, real problem we scoped, these are its real edges, and here is what comes next.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- State the finished architecture in one pass, end to end

```
ORIGIN:         SQLPROD01, 9 years old, single server, no secondary
                copy anywhere -- a ~48-hour outage, 12 missed ship
                dates, ~6 hours of avoidable changeovers on one line
HA:             BrennanWSFC (SQLDBA01/SQLDBA02) carrying BrennanAG,
                synchronous-commit, automatic failover, reachable
                through BrennanAGListener -- proven with real drills
PERFORMANCE:    WorkOrders report fixed (~52s to ~0.4s); Query Store
                baseline captured, pre- and post-cutover
AUTOMATION:     dbatools-driven backup, restore-verification, and
                maintenance jobs on both nodes, fully scheduled
OFF-SITE:       Every backup also lands in brennansqlbackups,
                independent of the building
MONITORING:     A Power BI dashboard covering replica health, job
                outcomes, and the AG-membership gap check
MULTI-PLATFORM: brennan-mongo-01 / iot_sensor_logs brought under real
                backups, monitoring, and a completed access review
DOCUMENTATION:  An AG failover runbook, a new-database checklist, and
                a platform inventory
INCIDENT FOUND & FIXED: ProductionSchedulingDB, created for the
                scheduling-module expansion, had its AG-join step
                scheduled for later and never actually finished. The
                first real planned failover drill found it, with the
                data itself completely safe but zero live orders at
                risk either way. Fixed, re-verified, and now backed
                by a recurring automated check.
```

Every line above was built, tested, and is now running in production -- that is the real, defensible claim this engagement gets to make.

## Step 2 -- Name what is still manual or unproven, specifically

```
GAP 1: The new-database checklist still depends on a human actually
  following it. Nothing in SQL Server stops a database from being
  created without it. The recurring AGMembershipCheck job is a real
  safety net, but it only catches a skipped step after the fact, on
  its next scheduled run -- not before the database goes live.

GAP 2: MongoDB's discipline is real but newer and less proven than
  the SQL Server side. brennan-mongo-01 has verified backups,
  monitoring, and a completed access review, but no replica set and
  no automatic failover. A hardware failure on that one server today
  means a real restore, measured in time, not a seconds-long failover.

GAP 3: Every failover tested on this project has been an in-cluster
  test -- one node down, the rest of the environment fully available.
  A true site-level disaster, the kind that depends on restoring from
  brennansqlbackups on new hardware, has a written RPO/RTO target from
  lesson 2 but has never actually been rehearsed end to end.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the honest one-paragraph summary for whoever reads this next

```
This engagement replaced a single nine-year-old server with no
secondary copy of its data with a clustered, automatically failed-
over, performance-tuned, automated, and off-site-backed-up SQL Server
environment, monitored on a live dashboard and documented well
enough for someone else to operate. It found and fixed a real
coverage gap along the way and brought a second platform, MongoDB,
under real DBA discipline. It did not build an automated gate around
new-database creation, give MongoDB the same failover protection
SQL Server now has, or run a true site-level disaster drill -- those
are real, named gaps for a future phase, not oversights pretending
not to exist.
```

## Step 4 -- Leave a short, prioritized list for a future phase

```
1. Run a true site-level disaster drill: simulate the whole building
   or BrennanWSFC itself being unavailable, and time an actual
   restore from brennansqlbackups against the lesson 2 RTO target.
   Closes Gap 3 -- the single highest-value item left, because it is
   the one failure mode nothing built so far has actually proven.
2. Add a lightweight gate (an Agent job trigger or a provisioning
   script check) that flags a brand-new, unprotected database the
   same day it is created, not on the next scheduled check. Closes
   Gap 1.
3. Scope whether brennan-mongo-01 needs a real replica set, based on
   how critical iot_sensor_logs becomes to the business. Closes Gap 2
   when and if the workload justifies the added complexity.
```

## Step 5 -- Close the series the way it should close: honestly, not triumphantly

This is the last video of twenty. Resist the pull to end on an unqualified victory lap. The real ending is: a genuinely dangerous single point of failure -- one aging server with no secondary copy and no tested recovery plan -- is gone, replaced by something clustered, automated, off-site-backed-up, and actually drilled, with a second platform brought into the same discipline along the way. One real gap was found and fixed in the process, which is a better outcome than an engagement that never finds out its gaps exist. Three honest, specific limitations remain, named and handed off instead of hidden. That is a finished engagement, not a perfect one -- and that is the whole point of telling it this way.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Closed the series with the full architecture laid out end to end -- the cluster and AG, performance tuning, automation, off-site backup, monitoring, MongoDB oversight, and documentation. Named three real gaps rather than glossing over them: the new-database checklist still depends on a human following it, MongoDB has no replica set or automatic failover yet, and no true site-level disaster drill -- only in-cluster failovers -- has ever been run.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Wrapped the engagement with an honest accounting of what shipped versus what is still open. The cluster, automation, and tested in-cluster failover are genuinely done -- that part is real. We also have a short, prioritized list for a future phase, led by finally running a true site-level disaster drill, so nothing gets rediscovered as a surprise later.
workplaceExplanation.executive: What we built is real: a modern, automated, tested database environment that survived its own practice disaster and came out stronger for it, now covering a second platform too. We are also telling you plainly what this does not cover yet -- the new-database checklist still needs a person to follow it, MongoDB does not yet have the same automatic failover SQL Server has, and we have never tested what happens if the whole building, not just one server, goes down. That is the honest finish line, not an oversold one.
